arXiv:2610.35748v2 [stat.ML] 12 Nov 2026

Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation
via Bellman Tournaments

Lars van der Laan Affiliation: Stanford University Email: vdlaan@stanford.edu    Vasilis Syrgkanis Affiliation: Stanford University    Nathan Kallus Affiliation: Netflix and Cornell University
Abstract

Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted QQ-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. For each candidate, PBV constructs critics from pairwise differences with the other candidates, using differences on the log scale for occupancy ratios. It then selects the candidate that minimizes the worst-case penalized score across these pairwise critics. The key insight motivating these pairwise critics is that QQ-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios serve as oracle critics whose moments against the Bellman and adjoint Bellman residuals control estimation error. The tournament criterion avoids the need to identify which pairwise critic best approximates the oracle critic, while the critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For QQ-function selection, we first propose unweighted PBV, which avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. We then develop importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit contraction of the Bellman operator under the target-policy occupancy measure, thereby avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, we propose adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees directly under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.

Keywords: Model selection, hyperparameter tuning, off-policy evaluation, Bellman equations, occupancy-ratio estimation, value-function estimation, infinite-horizon reinforcement learning

1.  Introduction

1.1.  Motivation

The goal of off-policy evaluation (OPE) is to estimate the value of a target policy using data collected under a different policy in a Markov decision process (MDP). In the infinite-horizon setting, two central objects in OPE are the target-policy action-value function, or QQ-function, and the discounted occupancy ratio (Uehara et al., 2026). The former gives the expected discounted cumulative reward from each state–action pair under the target policy, while the latter reweights the logged state–action distribution to the target policy’s discounted state–action distribution. These functions underlie direct, importance-weighted, and doubly robust OPE, as well as semiparametrically efficient inference (Jiang and Li, 2016; Xie et al., 2019; Kallus and Uehara, 2020; Kallus and Uehara, 2022; van der Laan et al., 2025). They are characterized, respectively, as fixed points of the Bellman and adjoint Bellman operators (Uehara et al., 2021). These fixed-point equations motivate fitted QQ-evaluation (FQE) for learning QQ-functions and fitted occupancy-ratio evaluation (FORE) for learning occupancy ratios (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008; van der Laan and Kallus, 2026). They also motivate minimax methods, such as DualDICE and minimax QQ-learning, which test Bellman or adjoint Bellman residuals against critic functions, that is, test functions used to detect violations of the corresponding equations (Nachum et al., 2019; Uehara et al., 2020; Uehara et al., 2021).

A central challenge in OPE is model selection and hyperparameter tuning. Different choices of algorithms, function classes, regularization, and hyperparameters produce competing QQ-function and occupancy-ratio estimates, but their estimation errors cannot be directly evaluated on held-out logged data. For QQ-functions, squared temporal-difference error is generally unsuitable for comparing candidates under stochastic transitions because it includes a candidate-dependent conditional-variance term (Baird III, 1995). Bellman-residual validation instead estimates the Bellman residual Q−ℬπ​QQ-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q for each candidate, where ℬπ\mathcal{B}_{\pi} denotes the target-policy Bellman operator, and selects the candidate with the smallest estimated mean-squared residual. However, estimating these residuals typically requires fitting a separate regression for each candidate (Zitovsky et al., 2023), which can be computationally prohibitive and introduces an additional tuning problem. An alternative is minimax Bellman-moment validation, which evaluates empirical moments of one-step temporal-difference residuals against a class of critic functions and selects the candidate that minimizes the largest absolute moment over that class (Uehara et al., 2021; Miyaguchi, 2026). This avoids separate Bellman-residual regressions but requires specifying and potentially tuning a critic class, and can involve computationally demanding and numerically delicate optimization, particularly with flexible critics.

For QQ-function selection, LSTD-Tournament (Liu et al., 2025) offers a simpler alternative that uses least-squares temporal-difference Q-learning (LSTDQ) to compare candidate QQ-functions pairwise. Its selection criterion can be viewed as a minimax Bellman-moment validation procedure that uses the candidate QQ-functions themselves as critics, avoiding the need to fit or tune a separate critic class. However, its theoretical guarantees depend on the conditioning of the pairwise LSTD matrices, and the resulting bounds can deteriorate when candidates are nearly collinear, as may occur when comparing similar hyperparameter settings.

1.2.  Contributions

We introduce pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods for selecting among finite classes of fitted QQ-functions and occupancy-ratio estimators using held-out transitions. We develop a new validation criterion based on critics constructed from pairwise differences between candidates, show how importance weighting relaxes the conditions needed for QQ-function selection, and extend the approach to occupancy-ratio selection. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification and near-collinearity among candidates.

Operationally, PBV evaluates each candidate using empirical moments of its Bellman or adjoint Bellman residual against critics constructed from pairwise differences with the other candidates. For occupancy ratios, these differences are taken on the log scale. For QQ-function selection, each moment is the held-out average of a one-step temporal-difference residual multiplied by a critic. PBV then uses a penalized tournament, subtracting a critic penalty from each absolute empirical moment and selecting the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score across all pairwise critics. Validation thus reduces to computing a finite collection of sample averages, without fitting auxiliary validation models or separately optimizing critic functions.

The motivation for these pairwise critics is that the estimation errors Qi−QπQ_{i}-Q^{\pi} and log⁡(wi/wπ)\log(w_{i}/w^{\pi}) serve as oracle critics for the Bellman and adjoint Bellman residuals, respectively. Under suitable conditions, we show that evaluating the Bellman residual of QiQ_{i} against Qi−QπQ_{i}-Q^{\pi} controls its squared L2L^{2} error, while evaluating the adjoint Bellman residual of wiw_{i} against log⁡(wi/wπ)\log(w_{i}/w^{\pi}) controls its generalized-KL error. The pairwise critics Qi−QjQ_{i}-Q_{j} and log⁡(wi/wj)\log(w_{i}/w_{j}) coincide with their oracle counterparts when the comparator equals the truth, and approximate them when the comparator is close to the truth. By taking the worst case over these pairwise critics, the tournament avoids the need to identify which comparator best approximates the truth, while the critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification.

For QQ-function selection, we first develop unweighted PBV, which evaluates pairwise Bellman moments under the offline distribution using a quadratic critic penalty. Because the target-policy Bellman operator need not be contractive in the corresponding L2L^{2} norm, our guarantees require a coercivity condition (Condition A2) on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. This condition plays a role similar to that of the matrix-conditioning assumptions in LSTD-Tournament and linear TD learning (Bradtke and Barto, 1996; Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997; Lagoudakis and Parr, 2003; Amortila et al., 2026). Unlike those assumptions, however, coercivity can hold even when candidate functions are nearly collinear. We then develop importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to evaluate the corresponding Bellman moments under the discounted target-occupancy distribution, where the Bellman operator is contractive. Thus, unweighted PBV avoids occupancy-ratio estimation but requires coercivity, whereas IW-PBV removes this requirement at the cost of estimating occupancy ratios.

For occupancy-ratio selection, we develop adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which evaluates adjoint Bellman residuals against log-ratio critics with a penalty proportional to the squared Hellinger distance between candidate ratios. A-PBV requires no importance weighting, coercivity, or matrix-conditioning assumptions, since the adjoint Bellman operator is contractive in KL divergence under the offline distribution (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026).

Finally, as contributions of independent interest, we extend the analysis of LSTD-Tournament to establish finite-sample oracle inequalities under candidate-class misspecification (Appendix N) and extend the method to occupancy-ratio selection (Appendix P). Both extensions require matrix-conditioning assumptions that IW-PBV and A-PBV, respectively, avoid.

1.3.  Related work

Model selection for QQ-functions and occupancy ratios. Existing OPE model-selection methods have focused primarily on QQ-functions, using Bellman residuals, candidate-dependent projections, nested classes, or auxiliary regressions and critics to replace the unavailable supervised loss (Farahmand and Szepesvári, 2011; Lee et al., 2022; Zitovsky et al., 2023; Miyaguchi, 2026). An early influential Bellman tournament method is BVFT (Xie and Jiang, 2021), which uses pairwise candidate-dependent state–action partitions and projected Bellman errors to select the QQ-function. BVFT-PE (Zhang and Jiang, 2021) extends this approach to policy evaluation. These approaches generally introduce additional estimation or structural requirements beyond the candidate class itself. PBV instead uses pairwise candidate differences directly as Bellman critics, avoiding state aggregation and allowing misspecified candidate classes. A more closely related approach is LSTD-Tournament (Liu et al., 2025), which also constructs pairwise validation criteria directly from the candidate class. We discuss this connection separately below.

By contrast, model selection among already-fitted occupancy-ratio estimators has received substantially less attention, despite extensive work on occupancy-ratio estimation (Nachum et al., 2019; Uehara et al., 2020; Uehara et al., 2021; van der Laan and Kallus, 2026). Our proposed A-PBV extends Bellman tournament methods to occupancy-ratio selection without coercivity or matrix-conditioning assumptions. For comparison, we also extend LSTD-Tournament to occupancy-ratio selection in Appendix P, but its guarantees require matrix-conditioning assumptions that A-PBV avoids. We describe the main validation methods in Section 3, with further discussion in Appendix Q.

Relation to LSTD-Tournament. Among our methods, unweighted PBV is most closely related to LSTD-Tournament (Liu et al., 2025). Although derived from pairwise LSTDQ, its selection criterion can be expressed as minimax Bellman-moment validation using the candidate QQ-functions themselves as critics. In contrast, PBV uses pairwise candidate differences as critics and introduces a quadratic penalty to accommodate misspecification. The theoretical guarantees for LSTD-Tournament require invertible pairwise LSTD matrices, with bounds that deteriorate as these matrices approach singularity.

In their numerical experiments, the authors instead use a candidate function and a pairwise difference as features, each normalized by its empirical standard deviation. Although (Qi,Qj)(Q_{i},Q_{j}) and (Qi,Qi−Qj)(Q_{i},Q_{i}-Q_{j}) span the same space, the latter representation can yield better-conditioned LSTD matrices after normalization. However, the authors do not provide finite-sample theoretical guarantees for this variant. We analyze the normalized selector in Appendix O and show that it can perform poorly when empirical critic standard deviations underestimate their population counterparts, as may occur when critics vary primarily on rare states missed by the validation sample (Proposition S40). This sensitivity is reflected in our finite-sample bound through the “spikiness” factor ‖f−𝔼ν​f‖∞2/‖f−𝔼ν​f‖2,ν2\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{\infty}^{2}/\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{2,\nu}^{2}, which must be uniformly bounded over the candidate functions and their pairwise differences; see Appendix A for additional discussion.

Unlike the empirical LSTD-Tournament criterion, unweighted PBV uses unnormalized pairwise differences as critics, together with quadratic penalties rather than empirical normalization. Our choice of pairwise differences is motivated by their role as approximations of oracle critics, rather than by numerical stability or matrix-conditioning considerations. Our guarantees do not require pairwise LSTD matrices to be invertible. Instead, we impose a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator along differences between each candidate and the best candidate. This condition can hold even when candidates are nearly collinear, without causing the constants in our error bounds to deteriorate (Section 5.1). IW-PBV removes the coercivity requirement altogether through importance weighting. In our experiments, unweighted PBV often outperforms LSTD-Tournament on Hopper and performs comparably on Deep OPE.

2.  OPE setup

2.1.  MDP and validation data

Consider a time-homogeneous Markov decision process with state space 𝒮\mathcal{S}, action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}, transition kernel P⁡(d​s′∣s,a)P(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\mid s,a), reward RR, and discount factor γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1). Write X=(S,A)X=(S,A) and let r⁡(x):=𝔼⁡[R∣X=x]r(x):=\mathbb{E}[R\mid X=x] denote the mean reward function. Fix a target policy π⁡(d​a∣s)\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s) and an initial state–action distribution d0d_{0}. The induced state–action transition kernel is Pπ(ds′,da′∣s,a):=P(ds′∣s,a)π(da′∣s′)P_{\pi}(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime},\mathrm{d}a^{\prime}\mid s,a):=P(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\pi(\mathrm{d}a^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime}). For any state–action function ff, define (π​f)​(s′):=∫f⁡(s′,a′)​π​(d​a′∣s′)(\pi f)(s^{\prime}):=\int f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime}) and (Pπ​f)​(s,a):=∫(π​f)​(s′)​P​(d​s′∣s,a)(P_{\pi}f)(s,a):=\int(\pi f)(s^{\prime})\,P(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\mid s,a). The goal of OPE is to estimate the discounted value Vπ:=𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​Rt∣X0∼d0]V^{\pi}:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{t}\mid X_{0}\sim d_{0}], where 𝔼π\mathbb{E}_{\pi} denotes expectation over trajectories generated by the MDP under π\pi and initialized from d0d_{0}.

For model selection, we use sample splitting. Candidate QQ-functions and occupancy-ratio estimates are fitted on a training sample and evaluated on an independent validation sample 𝒟n:={(Xt,Rt,St′)}t=1n\mathcal{D}_{n}:=\{(X_{t},R_{t},S_{t}^{\prime})\}_{t=1}^{n}. We condition on the training sample and assume that (Xt)t≥1(X_{t})_{t\geq 1} is a stationary Markov chain with invariant offline distribution ν\nu. This setting includes stationary trajectories generated by a stationary behavior policy b⁡(d​a∣s)b(\mathrm{d}a\mid s), as well as independently sampled transitions. In either case, conditional on the observed history through XtX_{t}, the law of (Rt,St′)(R_{t},S_{t}^{\prime}) is the one-step MDP law at XtX_{t}. For any state–action distribution ρ\rho, square-integrable functions f,gf,g, and positive integer mm, write ⟨f,g⟩ρ:=𝔼ρ​[f⁡(X)​g​(X)]\langle f,g\rangle_{\rho}:=\mathbb{E}_{\rho}[f(X)g(X)] and ‖f‖2,ρ:=⟨f,f⟩ρ1/2\|f\|_{2,\rho}:=\langle f,f\rangle_{\rho}^{1/2}, and set [m]:={1,…,m}[m]:=\{1,\ldots,m\}.

2.2.  Bellman and adjoint Bellman equations

The two nuisance functions we study are the target QQ-function and the discounted occupancy ratio. Both can be used to express the policy value and satisfy the Bellman and adjoint Bellman equations, respectively. The target QQ-function is defined by Qπ​(x):=𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​Rt|X0=x]Q^{\pi}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{t}\,|\,X_{0}=x]. It gives the policy value Vπ=𝔼d0​[Qπ​(X)]V^{\pi}=\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[Q^{\pi}(X)] and satisfies the Bellman fixed-point equation

Qπ=ℬπ​Qπ,ℬπ​Q:=r+γ​Pπ​Q,Q^{\pi}=\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q^{\pi},\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q:=r+\gamma P_{\pi}Q, (1)

where ℬπ\mathcal{B}_{\pi} is the Bellman operator (Sutton and Barto, 1998).

The normalized discounted occupancy ratio is defined by

wπ:=d​dπ,γd​ν,dπ,γ:=(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​ℒπ​(Xt),X0∼d0,w^{\pi}:=\frac{\mathrm{d}d_{\pi,\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}\nu},\hskip 18.49988ptd_{\pi,\gamma}:=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(X_{t}),\hskip 18.49988ptX_{0}\sim d_{0},

where ℒπ​(Xt)\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(X_{t}) denotes the marginal law of XtX_{t} under the target policy. We assume dπ,γ≪νd_{\pi,\gamma}\ll\nu. The occupancy ratio also gives the policy value through Vπ=(1−γ)−1​𝔼dπ,γ​[r⁡(X)]=(1−γ)−1​𝔼ν​[wπ​(X)​r​(X)]V^{\pi}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{d_{\pi,\gamma}}[r(X)]=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[w^{\pi}(X)r(X)]. Moreover, it satisfies the adjoint Bellman fixed-point equation (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026)

ℬπ∗​wπ=wπ,ℬπ∗​w:=(1−γ)​d​d0d​ν+γ​Pπ∗​w,Pπ∗​w:=d​{(w​ν)​Pπ}d​ν,\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w^{\pi}=w^{\pi},\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w:=(1-\gamma)\frac{\mathrm{d}d_{0}}{\mathrm{d}\nu}+\gamma P_{\pi}^{\ast}w,\hskip 18.49988ptP_{\pi}^{\ast}w:=\frac{\mathrm{d}\{(w\nu)P_{\pi}\}}{\mathrm{d}\nu}, (2)

which follows from the occupancy identity dπ,γ=(1−γ)​d0+γ​dπ,γ​Pπd_{\pi,\gamma}=(1-\gamma)d_{0}+\gamma d_{\pi,\gamma}P_{\pi} (Nachum et al., 2019). The term “adjoint” refers to the fact that Pπ∗P_{\pi}^{\ast} is the adjoint of PπP_{\pi} under the ν\nu-inner product: ⟨Pπ∗​w,Q⟩ν=⟨w,Pπ​Q⟩ν\langle P_{\pi}^{\ast}w,Q\rangle_{\nu}=\langle w,P_{\pi}Q\rangle_{\nu} (Uehara et al., 2021).

3.  Motivation and key ideas for pairwise Bellman validation

We begin by reviewing existing validation approaches for QQ-function selection, then develop the key ideas behind PBV. Section 4 presents the algorithms, including occupancy-ratio selection.

3.1.  Existing validation criteria

Let Q1,…,QKQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{K} be a finite class of candidate QQ-functions fitted on the training sample. A natural approach, which we refer to as Bellman-residual validation, selects a candidate by minimizing the mean-squared Bellman residual under the offline distribution ν\nu (Antos et al., 2008; Farahmand and Szepesvári, 2011):

ℒBR​(Q):=‖Q−ℬπ​Q‖2,ν2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BR}}(Q):=\|Q-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q\|_{2,\nu}^{2}.

Because QπQ^{\pi} is a Bellman fixed point, ℒBR​(Qπ)=0\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BR}}(Q^{\pi})=0, so the minimum over a class containing QπQ^{\pi} is attained at QπQ^{\pi}. The criterion is not directly estimable because (ℬπ​Q)​(X)(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q)(X) depends on unknown conditional laws. Without an MDP model, evaluating it generally requires estimating the Bellman residual Qi−ℬπ​QiQ_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}, for example by separately regressing Qi​(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(S′)Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S^{\prime}) on XX for each candidate (Zitovsky et al., 2023). This introduces additional computation, tuning, and estimation error.

A tempting alternative is to select candidates by minimizing the mean-squared one-step temporal-difference (TD) error (Sutton, 1988):

ℒTD​(Q):=𝔼ν​[{Q⁡(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Q)​(S′)}2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TD}}(Q):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\{Q(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q)(S^{\prime})\}^{2}\right].

Unlike the mean-squared Bellman residual, this criterion can be estimated directly from held-out transitions. Although the TD residual is conditionally unbiased for the Bellman residual, 𝔼⁡[Q⁡(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Q)​(S′)∣X]=Q⁡(X)−(ℬπ​Q)​(X)\mathbb{E}[Q(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q)(S^{\prime})\mid X]=Q(X)-(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q)(X), squaring introduces a conditional-variance term into the objective:

ℒTD​(Q)=ℒBR​(Q)+𝔼ν​[Var⁡(R+γ⁡(π​Q)​(S′)|X)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TD}}(Q)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BR}}(Q)+\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(R+\gamma(\pi Q)(S^{\prime})\,\middle|\,X\right)\right].

For γ>0\gamma>0 and stochastic transitions, this term generally depends on QQ, so minimizing squared TD error need not minimize the Bellman-residual error ℒBR​(Q)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BR}}(Q) or select QπQ^{\pi}, even when it belongs to the candidate class (Zitovsky et al., 2023). Directly estimating the squared Bellman residual without this variance term encounters the classical double-sampling obstruction: unbiased estimation generally requires two conditionally independent targets at the same state–action pair (Baird III, 1995; Feng et al., 2019).

A natural way around the double-sampling obstruction is to construct a minimax criterion based on moments of the Bellman residual against critic functions (Antos et al., 2008; Feng et al., 2019; Uehara et al., 2020; Zanette and Wainwright, 2022). Since QπQ^{\pi} is a Bellman fixed point, ⟨f,Qπ−ℬπ​Qπ⟩ν=0\langle f,Q^{\pi}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q^{\pi}\rangle_{\nu}=0 for every suitable critic ff. These moments can be estimated directly from one-step transitions because

𝔼ν​[f⁡(X)​{Q⁡(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Q)​(S′)}]=⟨f,Q−ℬπ​Q⟩ν.\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f(X)\{Q(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q)(S^{\prime})\}]=\langle f,Q-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q\rangle_{\nu}.

Given a critic class ℱ\mathcal{F}, this motivates the minimax population criterion

ℒℱ(Q):=supf∈ℱ:‖f‖2,ν≤1|𝔼ν[f(X){Q(X)−R−γ(πQ)(S′)}]|,\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{F}}(Q):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}:\ \|f\|_{2,\nu}\leq 1}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[f(X)\{Q(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q)(S^{\prime})\}\right]\right|,

which measures the largest violation of the Bellman moment conditions over the critic class.

We refer to model selection based on an empirical analogue of this criterion as minimax Bellman-moment validation. The main practical challenge is choosing a critic class ℱ\mathcal{F} for which these moments distinguish among candidate QQ-functions. If ℱ\mathcal{F} contains the normalized Bellman residual (Qi−ℬπ​Qi)/‖Qi−ℬπ​Qi‖2,ν(Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i})/\|Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\|_{2,\nu} for each i∈[K]i\in[K] with nonzero residual, then Cauchy–Schwarz and inclusion of this critic give ℒℱ​(Qi)=‖Qi−ℬπ​Qi‖2,ν\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{F}}(Q_{i})=\|Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\|_{2,\nu} (Uehara et al., 2021). Thus, minimax Bellman-moment validation can recover Bellman-residual validation without directly estimating ℬπ​Qi\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}. However, these ideal critics depend on the unknown Bellman residuals. In practice, restrictive critic classes may fail to distinguish among candidates, whereas richer classes increase statistical and computational complexity (Uehara et al., 2020; Zanette and Wainwright, 2022).

LSTD-Tournament (Liu et al., 2025) offers a simple alternative that avoids choosing a separate critic class by comparing candidate QQ-functions using pairwise LSTDQ. Its unnormalized selection criterion can be expressed as a minimax Bellman-moment criterion with the candidate QQ-functions themselves as critics. Specifically, for a finite candidate class {Q1,…,QK}\{Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{K}\}, the selector is

i^=arg⁡mini∈[K]​maxj∈[K]​|1n​∑t=1nQj​(Xt)​{Qi​(Xt)−Rt−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(St′)}|.\widehat{i}=\arg\min_{i\in[K]}\max_{j\in[K]}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}Q_{j}(X_{t})\left\{Q_{i}(X_{t})-R_{t}-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S_{t}^{\prime})\right\}\right|. (3)

Its theoretical guarantees require invertibility of the pairwise LSTD matrices, and the corresponding bounds can deteriorate under poor conditioning, as may occur when candidates are nearly collinear. We discuss these limitations and the normalization variant used in the authors’ experiments in Section 1.3 and Appendix A.

3.2.  Key ideas behind PBV

We develop a penalized Bellman tournament that uses pairwise differences between candidate QQ-functions as critics, rather than the candidate functions themselves. The following three observations motivate this construction and the algorithms in Section 4.

The first observation is that the estimation error Δi:=Qi−Qπ\Delta_{i}:=Q_{i}-Q^{\pi} defines an oracle critic whose Bellman moment is a quadratic form in Δi\Delta_{i}. This leads to the oracle criterion

ℒ⋆​(Qi)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\star}(Q_{i}) :=|𝔼ν​[Δi​(X)​{Qi​(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(S′)}]|\displaystyle:=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\Delta_{i}(X)\left\{Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S^{\prime})\right\}\right]\right|
=|⟨Δi,Qi−ℬπ​Qi⟩ν|=|⟨Δi,(I−γ​Pπ)​Δi⟩ν|,\displaystyle=\left|\langle\Delta_{i},Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\rangle_{\nu}\right|=\left|\langle\Delta_{i},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})\Delta_{i}\rangle_{\nu}\right|,

where the final equality follows from the fixed-point identity ℬπ​Qπ=Qπ\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q^{\pi}=Q^{\pi}. Unlike squared Bellman-residual criteria, ℒ⋆​(Qi)\mathcal{L}^{\star}(Q_{i}) is the absolute value of a Bellman moment and, if Δi\Delta_{i} were known, could be estimated directly from one-step transitions without estimating ℬπ​Qi\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}.

The oracle criterion controls squared estimation error when the Bellman quadratic form satisfies a coercivity condition. Specifically, suppose that, for some κν>0\kappa_{\nu}>0 and every i∈[K]i\in[K],

|⟨Δi,(I−γ​Pπ)​Δi⟩ν|≥κν​‖Δi‖2,ν2.\left|\langle\Delta_{i},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})\Delta_{i}\rangle_{\nu}\right|\geq\kappa_{\nu}\|\Delta_{i}\|_{2,\nu}^{2}. (4)

A corresponding upper bound holds under the standard one-step concentrability condition Cν,π:=‖d⁡(ν​Pπ)/d​ν‖∞<∞C_{\nu,\pi}:=\|\mathrm{d}(\nu P_{\pi})/\mathrm{d}\nu\|_{\infty}<\infty. By Cauchy–Schwarz and Jensen’s inequality, for every i∈[K]i\in[K],

|⟨Δi,(I−γ​Pπ)​Δi⟩ν|≤(1+γ​Cν,π)​‖Δi‖2,ν2.\left|\langle\Delta_{i},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})\Delta_{i}\rangle_{\nu}\right|\leq(1+\gamma\sqrt{C_{\nu,\pi}})\|\Delta_{i}\|_{2,\nu}^{2}.

Thus, under (4) and one-step concentrability, ℒ⋆​(Qi)\mathcal{L}^{\star}(Q_{i}) is comparable to ‖Δi‖2,ν2\|\Delta_{i}\|_{2,\nu}^{2} up to constant factors. Consequently, minimizing the oracle criterion yields an L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) error within a factor {(1+γ​Cν,π)/κν}1/2\{(1+\gamma\sqrt{C_{\nu,\pi}})/\kappa_{\nu}\}^{1/2} of the best candidate’s error mini∈[K]⁡‖Qi−Qπ‖2,ν\min_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu}.

The second observation is that pairwise differences between candidate QQ-functions can approximate the unknown oracle critics. For any i,j∈[K]i,j\in[K], write hi​j:=Qi−Qj=Δi−Δjh_{ij}:=Q_{i}-Q_{j}=\Delta_{i}-\Delta_{j}. Under realizability, there exists i⋆∈[K]i^{\star}\in[K] such that Qi⋆=QπQ_{i^{\star}}=Q^{\pi}, so hi​i⋆=Δih_{ii^{\star}}=\Delta_{i} exactly. More generally, comparison with a candidate close to QπQ^{\pi} provides an accurate approximation to the oracle critic Δi\Delta_{i}. Because the best comparator is unknown, we evaluate each candidate against all KK pairwise critics and take the largest penalized Bellman moment as its worst-case score. The population version of unweighted PBV selects

arg⁡mini∈[K]​maxj∈[K]​{|⟨hi​j,Qi−ℬπ​Qi⟩ν|−14​|⟨hi​j,(I−γ​Pπ)​hi​j⟩ν|}.\arg\min_{i\in[K]}\max_{j\in[K]}\left\{\left|\langle h_{ij},Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\rangle_{\nu}\right|-\frac{1}{4}\left|\langle h_{ij},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})h_{ij}\rangle_{\nu}\right|\right\}.

Unlike LSTD-Tournament in (3), this criterion uses pairwise differences rather than the candidate functions themselves as critics. Under realizability and coercivity, the unpenalized tournament already recovers QπQ^{\pi}, since the true candidate has a worst-case score of zero and comparison with it detects the error of every other candidate. Under misspecification, however, even the best candidate has a nonzero Bellman residual, and poor comparators can inflate its worst-case score. The quadratic penalty limits this inflation because the Bellman moment grows at most linearly with critic size, whereas the penalty grows quadratically, thereby enabling oracle guarantees under misspecification.

The guarantee for unweighted PBV under misspecification, however, relies on a variant of the coercivity condition in (4), requiring a positive lower bound along differences between each candidate and the best available candidate. This condition depends on the relationship between the offline distribution ν\nu and the target-policy dynamics and is related to, but distinct from, the matrix-conditioning assumptions of linear TD learning and LSTD-Tournament (Amortila et al., 2026) (see Section 5.1 for a comparison). A simple, albeit overly strong, sufficient condition is ‖Pπ​h‖2,ν≤c​‖h‖2,ν\|P_{\pi}h\|_{2,\nu}\leq c\|h\|_{2,\nu} for every such difference hh and some cc satisfying γ​c<1\gamma c<1. By Cauchy–Schwarz, this gives the required lower bound with κν=1−γ​c\kappa_{\nu}=1-\gamma c. Under one-step concentrability, one may take c=Cν,πc=\sqrt{C_{\nu,\pi}}, so the condition holds whenever γ2​Cν,π<1\gamma^{2}C_{\nu,\pi}<1. In particular, under stationary on-policy sampling, Cν,π=1C_{\nu,\pi}=1 and PπP_{\pi} is an L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) contraction, so the condition holds automatically with κν=1−γ\kappa_{\nu}=1-\gamma. Under distribution shift, however, coercivity need not hold.

The third observation is that the coercivity requirement under the offline distribution can be avoided by weighting each Bellman moment by wπ=d​dπ,γ/d​νw^{\pi}=\mathrm{d}d_{\pi,\gamma}/\mathrm{d}\nu. This weighting evaluates Bellman moments under the discounted target-occupancy distribution, with respect to which γ​Pπ\gamma P_{\pi} is a γ\sqrt{\gamma}-contraction in L2​(dπ,γ)L^{2}(d_{\pi,\gamma}) (van der Laan and Kallus, 2025b; Gelada and Bellemare, 2019). Consequently,

(1−γ)​‖Δi‖2,dπ,γ2≤⟨Δi,(I−γ​Pπ)​Δi⟩dπ,γ≤(1+γ)​‖Δi‖2,dπ,γ2.(1-\sqrt{\gamma})\|\Delta_{i}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}^{2}\leq\langle\Delta_{i},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})\Delta_{i}\rangle_{d_{\pi,\gamma}}\leq(1+\sqrt{\gamma})\|\Delta_{i}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}^{2}. (5)

Thus, the weighted oracle criterion controls mean-squared QQ-function error under the discounted target occupancy without requiring (4). Combining importance weighting with pairwise-difference critics and the same quadratic penalty as unweighted PBV yields the population version of importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV), which selects

arg⁡mini∈[K]​maxj∈[K]​{|⟨hi​j,Qi−ℬπ​Qi⟩dπ,γ|−14​|⟨hi​j,(I−γ​Pπ)​hi​j⟩dπ,γ|}.\arg\min_{i\in[K]}\max_{j\in[K]}\left\{\left|\langle h_{ij},Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\rangle_{d_{\pi,\gamma}}\right|-\frac{1}{4}\left|\langle h_{ij},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})h_{ij}\rangle_{d_{\pi,\gamma}}\right|\right\}.

The contraction inequality ensures that the quadratic penalty controls critic size without an additional coercivity assumption. The tradeoff is that the occupancy ratio wπw^{\pi} must be estimated sufficiently accurately, introducing an additional model-selection problem that we address using adjoint PBV in the next section.

4.  Pairwise Bellman validation algorithms

We now present the empirical unweighted PBV and IW-PBV selectors for QQ-function selection, along with A-PBV for occupancy-ratio selection.

For both QQ-function selectors, we also include Q0≡0Q_{0}\equiv 0 as an additional comparator, but not as a candidate for selection. This augmentation adds each QiQ_{i} to the set of pairwise-difference critics, since Qi−Q0=QiQ_{i}-Q_{0}=Q_{i}, and improved performance in our experiments (Appendix G.6).

4.1.  Unweighted PBV

For i∈[K]i\in[K] and 0≤j≤K0\leq j\leq K, let hi​j:=Qi−Qjh_{ij}:=Q_{i}-Q_{j}. We define the unweighted PBV scores and selector by

ℳ^i​junw\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{ij}^{\mathrm{unw}} :=|1n​∑t=1nhi​j​(Xt)​{Qi​(Xt)−Rt−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(St′)}|\displaystyle:=\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}h_{ij}(X_{t})\{Q_{i}(X_{t})-R_{t}-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S_{t}^{\prime})\}\right|
−14​|1n​∑t=1nhi​j​(Xt)​{hi​j​(Xt)−γ⁡(π​hi​j)​(St′)}|,\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt-\frac{1}{4}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}h_{ij}(X_{t})\{h_{ij}(X_{t})-\gamma(\pi h_{ij})(S_{t}^{\prime})\}\right|,
i^Qunw\displaystyle\widehat{i}_{Q}^{\mathrm{unw}} :=min⁡arg⁡min1≤i≤K​max0≤j≤K​ℳ^i​junw,\displaystyle:=\min\arg\min_{1\leq i\leq K}\max_{0\leq j\leq K}\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{ij}^{\mathrm{unw}}, (6)

where both moments are evaluated under the offline distribution, with absolute values taken after averaging. By iterated expectation, the population penalty is 14​|⟨hi​j,(I−γ​Pπ)​hi​j⟩ν|\frac{1}{4}|\langle h_{ij},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})h_{ij}\rangle_{\nu}|, which, under Condition A2, is bounded below by 14​κν​‖hi​k⋆‖2,ν2\frac{1}{4}\kappa_{\nu}\|h_{ik^{\star}}\|_{2,\nu}^{2} when j=k⋆j=k^{\star}. Using the absolute quadratic form rather than its lower bound avoids the need to know κν\kappa_{\nu}. More generally, the penalty coefficient can be any λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1); the choice λ=1/4\lambda=1/4 minimizes the multiplicative constant in our population oracle bound.

4.2.  Adjoint PBV and importance-weighted PBV

To implement IW-PBV, we first introduce adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which applies pairwise validation to the adjoint Bellman equation to select an occupancy-ratio estimator. We summarize the construction here and defer further details and intuition to Appendix B. As in the QQ-function case, adjoint Bellman moments for fixed critics can be estimated directly from one-step transitions and independent draws from d0d_{0} (Nachum et al., 2019).

For nonnegative integrable functions pp and qq, define the generalized KL divergence

𝖣ν(p∥q):=𝔼ν[p(X)logp⁡(X)q⁡(X)−p(X)+q(X)].\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(p\|q):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[p(X)\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}-p(X)+q(X)\right].

Unlike the usual KL divergence, 𝖣ν\mathsf{D}_{\nu} does not require pp and qq to integrate to one and therefore permits unnormalized ratio candidates. When the three divergences below are finite, the Bregman three-point identity (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017), together with contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator in generalized KL divergence (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026), gives

⟨w−ℬπ∗​w,log⁡(w/wπ)⟩ν\displaystyle\left\langle w-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w,\log(w/w^{\pi})\right\rangle_{\nu} =𝖣ν(w∥wπ)−𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥wπ)+𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥w)\displaystyle=\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi})-\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w^{\pi})+\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w)
≥(1−γ)𝖣ν(w∥wπ).\displaystyle\geq(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi}).

Thus, log⁡(w/wπ)\log(w/w^{\pi}) provides an oracle critic whose adjoint Bellman moment controls generalized-KL error. Given MM candidate occupancy ratios w1,…,wMw_{1},\ldots,w_{M}, we approximate this critic using pairwise log-ratios ℓa​b:=log⁡(wa/wb)\ell_{ab}:=\log(w_{a}/w_{b}).

As in unweighted PBV, we penalize pairwise moments to control the influence of inaccurate comparators under misspecification. We use Hellinger and Bellman quadratic penalties for A-PBV and IW-PBV, respectively. Let X0,1,…,X0,nX_{0,1},\ldots,X_{0,n} be independent draws from d0d_{0}.11 1 If expectations under d0d_{0} are known, the corresponding empirical averages can be replaced by their population values. Define the penalized empirical pairwise scores

𝒮^a​badj\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{ab}^{\mathrm{adj}} :=|1n​∑t=1nwa​(Xt)​{ℓa​b​(Xt)−γ⁡(π​ℓa​b)​(St′)}−1−γn​∑t=1nℓa​b​(X0,t)|\displaystyle:=\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}w_{a}(X_{t})\{\ell_{ab}(X_{t})-\gamma(\pi\ell_{ab})(S_{t}^{\prime})\}-\frac{1-\gamma}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\ell_{ab}(X_{0,t})\right|
−1−γ4​n∑t=1n{wa​(Xt)−wb​(Xt)}2,\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt-\frac{1-\gamma}{4n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\{\sqrt{w_{a}(X_{t})}-\sqrt{w_{b}(X_{t})}\}^{2},
ℳ^i​jIW​(w)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{ij}^{\mathrm{IW}}(w) :=|1n​∑t=1nw⁡(Xt)​hi​j​(Xt)​{Qi​(Xt)−Rt−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(St′)}|\displaystyle:=\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}w(X_{t})h_{ij}(X_{t})\{Q_{i}(X_{t})-R_{t}-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S_{t}^{\prime})\}\right|
−14​|1n​∑t=1nw⁡(Xt)​hi​j​(Xt)​{hi​j​(Xt)−γ⁡(π​hi​j)​(St′)}|.\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt-\frac{1}{4}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}w(X_{t})h_{ij}(X_{t})\{h_{ij}(X_{t})-\gamma(\pi h_{ij})(S_{t}^{\prime})\}\right|.

The IW-PBV penalty uses the same quadratic form as unweighted PBV, but weighted by the fitted occupancy ratio. We combine the two stages in Algorithm 1, which evaluates M2+K⁡(K+1)M^{2}+K(K+1) pairwise scores without fitting additional validation models or critics.

To improve finite-sample stability, we recommend screening out occupancy-ratio candidates with excessively concentrated weights, using the effective sample size (ESS) diagnostic (Metelli et al., 2020; Zenati et al., 2025). For a candidate wkw_{k}, its empirical ESS is

ESS^​(wk):=nw​(ℙn,w​wk)2ℙn,w​wk2,\widehat{\mathrm{ESS}}(w_{k}):=n_{w}\frac{(\mathbb{P}_{n,w}w_{k})^{2}}{\mathbb{P}_{n,w}w_{k}^{2}},

where ℙn,w\mathbb{P}_{n,w} averages over the nwn_{w} ratio-training state–action observations. Candidates with ESS^​(wk)/nw\widehat{\mathrm{ESS}}(w_{k})/n_{w} below a prespecified threshold can be excluded to mitigate instability from extreme ratio estimates; a practical default is 0.010.01 or 0.050.05. We also recommend tempering the selected occupancy ratio w^\widehat{w} for downstream weighting, following Sinha et al. (2022), as

w~​(x):=w^​(x)1/Tℙn,w​w^1/T,T≥1,\widetilde{w}(x):=\frac{\widehat{w}(x)^{1/T}}{\mathbb{P}_{n,w}\widehat{w}^{1/T}},\hskip 18.49988ptT\geq 1,

where larger TT reduces the concentration of the weights. As T→∞T\to\infty, the tempered weights converge to one, and tempered IW-PBV reduces to unweighted PBV. Because unweighted PBV does not require estimating an occupancy ratio, it may be preferable when reliable importance weighting is difficult. Truncation of importance weights can also be important for downstream policy-value estimation (Mehrabi and Wager, 2024).

We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities for unweighted PBV and the two-stage procedure combining A-PBV and IW-PBV. Write (Pb​f)​(x):=𝔼⁡[f⁡(Xt+1)∣Xt=x](P_{b}f)(x):=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+1})\mid X_{t}=x] for the validation chain’s transition operator. For independent transitions, (Pb​f)​(x)=𝔼ν​[f⁡(X)](P_{b}f)(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f(X)], so Condition A1 holds with gb=1g_{b}=1.

However, this formal implication does not account for the constants appearing in the respective finite-sample bounds. In particular, coercivity only guarantees a lower bound of order κν2​‖hi​k⋆‖2,ν4\kappa_{\nu}^{2}\|h_{ik^{\star}}\|_{2,\nu}^{4} on the squared LSTD moments. 5.2.  Adjoint PBV and importance-weighted PBV

We next establish guarantees for the two-stage procedure, which estimates the discounted occupancy ratio to avoid imposing coercivity under the offline distribution. We measure occupancy-ratio estimation error using the Hellinger distance Hν​(p,q):=‖p−q‖2,νH_{\nu}(p,q):=\|\sqrt{p}-\sqrt{q}\|_{2,\nu}, defined for nonnegative integrable functions pp and qq. For A-PBV, we assume one-step coverage and bounded ratio candidates, which ensure that the pairwise log-ratio critics are uniformly bounded.

Unlike unweighted PBV, IW-PBV provides a QQ-function error guarantee without imposing coercivity under the offline distribution. The bound separates candidate approximation error, validation error, and error from occupancy-ratio estimation. The horizon dependence is (1−γ)−1/2(1-\gamma)^{-1/2} for QQ-function approximation, (1−γ)−1(1-\gamma)^{-1} for direct validation error, and (1−γ)−3/2(1-\gamma)^{-3/2} for occupancy-ratio estimation error. 6.  Experiments

We evaluate unweighted PBV and IW-PBV on two benchmarks: the released Hopper benchmark of Liu et al. (2025), and four MuJoCo environments using DeepOPE target policies and D4RL offline datasets (Fu et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2020). To assess target-occupancy weighting under controlled overlap, we also collect logging data by sampling one benchmark policy uniformly at the start of each trajectory and following it until termination. Each component policy is evaluated in turn as the target, so the expected fraction of trajectories following the target policy is 1/101/10 for Hopper and 1/111/11 for DeepOPE.

On Hopper, we use the released offline transitions, candidate predictions, and reference values. These include 60 model-free settings on the main gravity and noise grids, 60 under poor coverage, and 36 model-based settings. The model-free and model-based candidate classes contain 15 and five candidates, respectively. For DeepOPE, four environments, five dataset qualities, and eleven target policies give 220 settings. We fit 60 neural FQE candidates per setting, varying network architecture, learning rate, and training duration. The controlled-overlap studies contain 60 Hopper and 44 DeepOPE settings, with 60 FQE candidates per setting.

For IW-PBV, we fit candidate occupancy ratios using fitted occupancy-ratio evaluation (FORE; van der Laan and Kallus, 2026) and select among them with A-PBV on independent data. Before selection, we discard candidates with training relative ESS below 5% and cap the remaining predictions at 50. Following Sinha et al. (2022), we temper the selected ratio with power 1/T1/T, using T=5T=5 and also reporting T=2T=2. We compare with the unnormalized and normalized-difference variants of LSTD-Tournament and with squared TD error, using identical candidates and validation draws. We report mean absolute policy-value error and initial-state value RMSE, with DeepOPE errors normalized by each environment’s range of reference policy values (Fu et al., 2021). Appendix G gives the evaluation details and additional results.

On the released Hopper benchmark, unweighted PBV has lower mean absolute policy-value error and initial-state value RMSE than both LSTD-Tournament variants in all three benchmark groups (Table 1). Under controlled overlap, IW-PBV with T=5T=5 has lower aggregate mean absolute policy-value error than unweighted PBV and both LSTD-Tournament variants at every validation sample size shown (Figure 1). Comparing the two temperatures, T=2T=2 gives lower mean value error at larger sample sizes in controlled Hopper and in the DeepOPE Hopper and Walker2d environments; T=5T=5 gives lower error in HalfCheetah. On full DeepOPE, unnormalized LSTD-Tournament has slightly lower aggregate errors, but the differences among the PBV and LSTD-Tournament variants are small relative to the overall error (Appendix G.8).

We study occupancy-ratio selection in Appendix H. In the controlled Hopper ratio experiment, A-PBV has lower aggregate Hellinger distance, ratio RMSE, generalized KL, and reward error than Adjoint LSTD-Tournament across three candidate libraries. However, using A-PBV rather than Adjoint LSTD-Tournament to select the occupancy ratio does not consistently improve downstream policy-value estimation with IW-PBV, with results varying across benchmarks. Compared with untempered weighting, tempering substantially reduces errors on the main model-free and model-based Hopper grids; its effect on DeepOPE depends on the benchmark and validation sample size.

7.  Discussion

Unweighted PBV avoids occupancy-ratio estimation and admits oracle guarantees under candidate-class misspecification, provided a coercivity condition holds. IW-PBV removes this requirement through marginalized importance weighting, at the cost of estimating occupancy ratios. For occupancy-ratio selection, we also develop A-PBV and Adjoint LSTD-Tournament, with the former avoiding matrix-conditioning assumptions. Our experiments show that unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, while the benefits of importance weighting depend on the setting, the accuracy of the estimated occupancy ratios, and the degree of tempering. In particular, more accurate occupancy-ratio estimates do not necessarily lead to more accurate downstream policy-value estimates, motivating tempering and truncation to manage the bias–variance tradeoff associated with importance weighting.

We extend PBV to projected QQ-functions and occupancy weights in Appendix E (van der Laan et al., 2025). We also extend PBV to soft optimal control in Appendix F using occupancy weighting and temperature annealing, building on van der Laan and Kallus (2025a).

AI use statement

Generative AI tools were used to assist with manuscript drafting and editing, as well as developing and checking mathematical proofs. In particular, these tools assisted with extending the finite-sample analysis of LSTD-Tournament to candidate-class misspecification (Appendix N) and developing its extension to occupancy-ratio selection (Appendix P). The authors independently verified all mathematical arguments and take full responsibility for the paper.

Appendix contents

Appendix A Comparison with LSTD-Tournament

Relative to normalized-difference LSTD-Tournament, unweighted PBV avoids dividing empirical moments by potentially small or inaccurately estimated critic standard deviations. When a critic has little variation relative to its magnitude, this normalization can amplify errors in the empirical moments. In Appendix O, we construct a counterexample where underestimating a critic’s standard deviation causes the normalized tournament to select a candidate with error bounded away from zero, even when the best available candidate has arbitrarily small error. For bounded candidates, Appendix O also establishes a finite-sample oracle inequality for the empirically normalized tournament under a matrix-conditioning assumption, but with a bound depending on both the “spikiness” measure ‖f−𝔼ν​f‖∞2/‖f−𝔼ν​f‖2,ν2\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{\infty}^{2}/\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{2,\nu}^{2} and the noise amplification factor ‖f‖2,ν/‖f−𝔼ν​f‖2,ν\|f\|_{2,\nu}/\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{2,\nu}, evaluated for candidates and pairwise differences f∈{Qi,Qi−Qj:i≠j}f\in\{Q_{i},Q_{i}-Q_{j}:\ i\neq j\}22 2 One can show that normalization by the norm ‖f‖2,ν\|f\|_{2,\nu} instead of the standard deviation ‖f−𝔼ν​f‖2,ν\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{2,\nu} avoids amplification from the latter factor but not from the former. . These quantities can be arbitrarily large even for uniformly bounded candidates. For example, if the candidate class contains Gaussian kernel bumps of bandwidth hh added to a nonzero constant, the spikiness measure can grow at rate h−dh^{-d} and the noise amplification factor at rate h−d/2h^{-d/2} as h→0h\to 0 in dd dimensions. Figure S1 illustrates both failure mechanisms for normalized LSTD-Tournament, as well as the failure mechanism for unnormalized LSTD-Tournament.

Appendix B Adjoint PBV for occupancy-ratio selection

The first stage of Algorithm 1 selects the discounted occupancy ratio used by its IW-PBV stage. We consider a finite class of candidates w1,…,wMw_{1},\ldots,w_{M} fitted on the training sample and, conditional on that sample, treat them as fixed and independent of the validation data. As in the QQ-function setting, we use a minimax criterion based on adjoint Bellman moments and construct the critics directly from the candidate class.

  1. (C1)

    Target-relative support and comparability. Let 𝒳π:={x:wπ​(x)>0}\mathcal{X}^{\pi}:=\{x:w^{\pi}(x)>0\}. Each candidate satisfies wi=0w_{i}=0 ν\nu-almost surely on (𝒳π)c(\mathcal{X}^{\pi})^{c}, and there exists Λw≥1\Lambda_{w}\geq 1 such that

    Λw−1≤wi​(X)wπ​(X)≤Λwν​-almost surely on ​𝒳π,i=1,…,M.\Lambda_{w}^{-1}\leq\frac{w_{i}(X)}{w^{\pi}(X)}\leq\Lambda_{w}\hskip 18.49988pt\nu\text{-almost surely on }\mathcal{X}^{\pi},\hskip 18.49988pti=1,\ldots,M.

B.1.  From oracle log-ratio critics to pairwise selection

For every bounded critic ff, the adjoint Bellman residual satisfies the moment identity (Nachum et al., 2019)

𝔼ν​[{w⁡(X)−(ℬπ∗​w)​(X)}​f​(X)]=𝔼ν​[w⁡(X)​{f⁡(X)−γ⁡(π​f)​(S′)}]−(1−γ)​𝔼d0​[f⁡(X)].\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\{w(X)-(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w)(X)\}f(X)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[w(X)\{f(X)-\gamma(\pi f)(S^{\prime})\}\right]-(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[f(X)]. (S1)

In particular, this moment vanishes at w=wπw=w^{\pi} for every bounded critic ff. We measure occupancy-ratio error using the generalized Kullback–Leibler divergence, defined for nonnegative integrable functions pp and qq by

𝖣ν(p∥q):=𝔼ν[p(X)logp⁡(X)q⁡(X)−p(X)+q(X)].\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(p\|q):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[p(X)\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}-p(X)+q(X)\right]. (S2)

Unlike the standard KL divergence, 𝖣ν\mathsf{D}_{\nu} does not require pp and qq to integrate to one and therefore accommodates unnormalized candidates. We use 0​log⁡(0/q)=00\log(0/q)=0 and p​log⁡(p/0)=+∞p\log(p/0)=+\infty for p>0p>0. The adjoint Bellman operator is a contraction in generalized KL divergence (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026):

𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥wπ)≤γ𝖣ν(w∥wπ).\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w^{\pi})\leq\gamma\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi}). (S3)

We therefore seek a critic whose adjoint Bellman moment directly controls generalized-KL error. In the QQ-function case, pairing the Bellman residual with Q−QπQ-Q^{\pi} yields a criterion comparable to squared L2L^{2} error. For occupancy ratios, the relevant error is generalized KL, which is the Bregman divergence generated pointwise by ϕ⁡(u)=u​log⁡u−u\phi(u)=u\log u-u:

𝖣ν(p∥q)=𝔼ν[ϕ{p(X)}−ϕ{q(X)}−ϕ′{q(X)}{p(X)−q(X)}],\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(p\|q)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\phi\{p(X)\}-\phi\{q(X)\}-\phi^{\prime}\{q(X)\}\{p(X)-q(X)\}\right],

Since ϕ′​(u)=log⁡u\phi^{\prime}(u)=\log u, the corresponding critic is ϕ′​{w⁡(X)}−ϕ′​{wπ​(X)}=log⁡{w⁡(X)/wπ​(X)}\phi^{\prime}\{w(X)\}-\phi^{\prime}\{w^{\pi}(X)\}=\log\{w(X)/w^{\pi}(X)\} (Amari and Nagaoka, 2000). By the Bregman three-point identity (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017),

𝔼ν​[{w⁡(X)−(ℬπ∗​w)​(X)}​{ϕ′​(w⁡(X))−ϕ′​(wπ​(X))}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\{w(X)-(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w)(X)\}\{\phi^{\prime}(w(X))-\phi^{\prime}(w^{\pi}(X))\}\right]
=𝖣ν(w∥wπ)−𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥wπ)+𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥w)\displaystyle=\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi})-\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w^{\pi})+\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w)
≥𝖣ν(w∥wπ)−𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥wπ).\displaystyle\geq\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi})-\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|w^{\pi}).

By this inequality and the contraction property of ℬπ∗\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast} in (S3),

𝔼ν[{w(X)−(ℬπ∗w)(X)}log{w(X)/wπ(X)}]≥(1−γ)𝖣ν(w∥wπ).\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\{w(X)-(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w)(X)\}\log\{w(X)/w^{\pi}(X)\}\right]\geq(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi}).

This motivates the oracle criterion

𝒮⋆​(w)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\star}(w) :=𝔼ν​[w⁡(X)​{log⁡w⁡(X)wπ​(X)−γ⁡(π​log⁡wwπ)​(S′)}]−(1−γ)​𝔼d0​[log⁡w⁡(X)wπ​(X)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[w(X)\left\{\log\frac{w(X)}{w^{\pi}(X)}-\gamma\left(\pi\log\frac{w}{w^{\pi}}\right)(S^{\prime})\right\}\right]-(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}\!\left[\log\frac{w(X)}{w^{\pi}(X)}\right], (S4)

which, by (S1), directly controls generalized-KL error. Unlike in the QQ-function case, the adjoint contraction holds under the offline distribution ν\nu, so no importance weighting or additional pairwise coercivity condition is required.

Under Condition C1, the pairwise log-ratio critics satisfy |log⁡{wi​(X)/wj​(X)}|≤2​log⁡Λw\left|\log\{w_{i}(X)/w_{j}(X)\}\right|\leq 2\log\Lambda_{w} ν\nu-almost surely for every i,j∈[M]i,j\in[M]. Under this boundedness, the following two-sided comparison holds.

Lemma S1 (Oracle log-ratio equivalence).

Suppose Condition C1 holds. Then, for every i∈{1,…,M}i\in\{1,\ldots,M\},

(1−γ)𝖣ν(wi∥wπ)≤𝒮⋆(wi)≤22Λw(1+γ)𝖣ν(wi∥wπ).(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w_{i}\|w^{\pi})\leq\mathcal{S}^{\star}(w_{i})\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,\Lambda_{w}(1+\sqrt{\gamma})\,\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w_{i}\|w^{\pi}). (S5)

By Lemma S1, a minimizer of the oracle score has generalized-KL error within a fixed factor of the best candidate in the class. The remaining obstacle is that the oracle critic log⁡(wi/wπ)\log(w_{i}/w^{\pi}) is unknown. As in the QQ-function construction, we replace it by pairwise critics from the candidate class. Define ℓi​j:=log⁡wiwj\ell_{ij}:=\log\frac{w_{i}}{w_{j}} and the corresponding pairwise score

𝒮i​j:=𝔼ν​[wi​(X)​{ℓi​j​(X)−γ⁡(π​ℓi​j)​(S′)}]−(1−γ)​𝔼d0​[ℓi​j​(X)].\mathcal{S}_{ij}:=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[w_{i}(X)\{\ell_{ij}(X)-\gamma(\pi\ell_{ij})(S^{\prime})\}\right]-(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[\ell_{ij}(X)].

We then select the candidate with the smallest worst-case score max1≤j≤M⁡|𝒮i​j|\max_{1\leq j\leq M}|\mathcal{S}_{ij}|. Under realizability, if wi⋆=wπw_{i^{\star}}=w^{\pi}, then ℓi​i⋆=log⁡(wi/wπ)\ell_{ii^{\star}}=\log(w_{i}/w^{\pi}) is the oracle critic and hence

max1≤j≤M|𝒮i​j|≥𝒮i​i⋆=𝒮⋆(wi)≥(1−γ)𝖣ν(wi∥wπ).\max_{1\leq j\leq M}|\mathcal{S}_{ij}|\geq\mathcal{S}_{ii^{\star}}=\mathcal{S}^{\star}(w_{i})\geq(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w_{i}\|w^{\pi}).

By contrast, 𝒮i⋆​j=0\mathcal{S}_{i^{\star}j}=0 for every jj, since wi⋆=wπw_{i^{\star}}=w^{\pi} satisfies the adjoint Bellman equation. Thus, minimizing the worst-case pairwise score recovers wπw^{\pi} under realizability.

B.2.  Penalized score and selector

The remaining challenge is misspecification. When wπw^{\pi} is not contained in the class, pairwise log ratios only approximate the oracle critics. We therefore penalize each pairwise score to account for the error from using a comparison candidate wjw_{j} in place of wπw^{\pi}. We use Hellinger distance because it provides a symmetric measure of separation between the two candidate ratios that can be controlled by their generalized-KL errors relative to wπw^{\pi}. For nonnegative pp and qq, define the squared Hellinger distance

Hν2​(p,q):=𝔼ν​[{p⁡(X)−q⁡(X)}2].H_{\nu}^{2}(p,q):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\{\sqrt{p(X)}-\sqrt{q(X)}\}^{2}\right].

For each ordered pair (i,j)(i,j), define the penalized population score

𝒮i​jadj:=|𝒮i​j|−1−γ4​Hν2​(wi,wj).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{ij}^{\mathrm{adj}}:=|\mathcal{S}_{ij}|-\frac{1-\gamma}{4}H_{\nu}^{2}(w_{i},w_{j}).

The factor 1−γ1-\gamma comes from the lower bound for the oracle score in (S5). The coefficient (1−γ)/4(1-\gamma)/4 allows the error from replacing the oracle critic by a pairwise critic to be absorbed in the oracle comparison. The A-PBV population selector is

i~w∈arg⁡min1≤i≤M​max1≤j≤M​𝒮i​jadj.\widetilde{i}_{w}\in\arg\min_{1\leq i\leq M}\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\mathcal{S}_{ij}^{\mathrm{adj}}.

To implement A-PBV, we evaluate empirical versions of the penalized pairwise scores using held-out one-step transitions {(Xt,St′)}t=1n\{(X_{t},S_{t}^{\prime})\}_{t=1}^{n} and independent initial state–action draws {X0,t}t=1n\{X_{0,t}\}_{t=1}^{n} from d0d_{0}. Algorithm S1 summarizes the resulting procedure, which requires only M2M^{2} directly computable pairwise scores and no additional nuisance or critic fitting.

𝖣ν(wi~w∥wπ)≤{4​2​Λw1−γ+23}​min1≤i≤M​𝖣ν(wi∥wπ).\sqrt{\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w_{\widetilde{i}_{w}}\|w^{\pi})}\leq\left\{\frac{4\sqrt{2}\,\Lambda_{w}}{1-\sqrt{\gamma}}+\frac{2}{3}\right\}\min_{1\leq i\leq M}\sqrt{\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w_{i}\|w^{\pi})}. (S6)

Appendix C Additional guarantees for QQ-function selection

We establish population and finite-sample guarantees for the importance-weighted and unweighted PBV selectors. Write 𝒥Q:={0,1,…,K}\mathcal{J}_{Q}:=\{0,1,\ldots,K\} for the comparator indices, with Q0≡0Q_{0}\equiv 0.

C.1.  Importance-weighted PBV

Population oracle inequality.

We justify IW-PBV’s quadratic penalty under candidate-class misspecification, extending the realizable argument in Section 3.2. We require only the following second-moment condition.

  1. (B1)

    Second moments under the target occupancy. The candidate functions and rewards satisfy

    max1≤i≤K⁡‖Qi‖2,dπ,γ2+𝔼ν​[wπ​(X)​R2]<∞.\max_{1\leq i\leq K}\|Q_{i}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[w^{\pi}(X)R^{2}]<\infty.

Condition B1 holds, for example, when the rewards and candidate functions are uniformly bounded.

Define the penalized population score ℳi​jIW:=|⟨hi​j,Qi−ℬπ​Qi⟩dπ,γ|−14​⟨hi​j,(I−γ​Pπ)​hi​j⟩dπ,γ\mathcal{M}_{ij}^{\mathrm{IW}}:=|\langle h_{ij},Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\rangle_{d_{\pi,\gamma}}|-\frac{1}{4}\langle h_{ij},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})h_{ij}\rangle_{d_{\pi,\gamma}} and let i~Q∈arg⁡mini∈[K]​maxj∈𝒥Q​ℳi​jIW\widetilde{i}_{Q}\in\arg\min_{i\in[K]}\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{Q}}\mathcal{M}_{ij}^{\mathrm{IW}}.

Theorem S4 (Population IW-PBV oracle inequality).

Suppose Condition B1 holds. Then every population minimizer i~Q\widetilde{i}_{Q} satisfies

‖Qi~Q−Qπ‖2,dπ,γ≤{1+2​1+γ1−γ}​min1≤i≤K​‖Qi−Qπ‖2,dπ,γ.\|Q_{\widetilde{i}_{Q}}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}\leq\left\{1+2\sqrt{\frac{1+\sqrt{\gamma}}{1-\sqrt{\gamma}}}\right\}\min_{1\leq i\leq K}\|Q_{i}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}. (S7)

Thus, every minimizer of the penalized population criterion has error within a factor depending only on γ\gamma of that of the best candidate, without requiring realizability. In particular, if QπQ^{\pi} belongs to the candidate class, every population minimizer equals QπQ^{\pi} in L2​(dπ,γ)L^{2}(d_{\pi,\gamma}).

Finite-sample oracle inequality.

We next account for the two additional sources of error in the practical selector: estimation of wπw^{\pi} and sampling variability in the pairwise scores computed on the validation sample. For each candidate, define the TD residual

εi:=Qi​(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(S′),i∈𝒥Q.\varepsilon_{i}:=Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S^{\prime}),\hskip 18.49988pti\in\mathcal{J}_{Q}.

In particular, ε0=−R\varepsilon_{0}=-R. The following conditions are also required for the finite-sample analysis.

  1. (B2)

    Bounded candidate differences and conditional TD means. There are finite constants HQH_{Q} and GQG_{Q} such that, almost surely,

    max0≤i,j≤K⁡|hi​j​(X)|≤HQ,max0≤i≤K⁡|𝔼⁡[εi∣X]|≤GQ.\displaystyle\max_{0\leq i,j\leq K}|h_{ij}(X)|\leq H_{Q},\hskip 18.49988pt\max_{0\leq i\leq K}\left|\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{i}\mid X]\right|\leq G_{Q}.
  2. (B3)

    Conditional subexponential TD noise. There is a finite constant σQ>0\sigma_{Q}>0 such that, almost surely,

    max0≤i≤K𝔼[exp{|εi−𝔼⁡[εi∣X]|σQ}|X]≤2.\displaystyle\max_{0\leq i\leq K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.\exp\left\{\frac{\left|\varepsilon_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{i}\mid X]\right|}{\sigma_{Q}}\right\}\right|X\right]\leq 2.

Under Condition A1, Bernstein concentration holds for the stationary validation process with effective sample size of order n​gbng_{b}. Independent validation transitions correspond to gb=1g_{b}=1 (Jiang et al., 2025). Under Condition B2, the candidate differences and the conditional means of the TD residuals are bounded. Under Condition B3, the centered TD residuals are conditionally subexponential; the residuals themselves need not be bounded. If |εi|≤G¯Q|\varepsilon_{i}|\leq\bar{G}_{Q} almost surely for every ii and some G¯Q>0\bar{G}_{Q}>0, then the conditional-mean bound in Condition B2 holds with GQ=G¯QG_{Q}=\bar{G}_{Q}, and Condition B3 holds with σQ=2​G¯Q/log⁡2\sigma_{Q}=2\bar{G}_{Q}/\log 2. Finally, the fitted-weight multiplier in the validation scores is bounded under Condition B4.

+CQ,wt1−γ​Hν​(w^,wπ)\displaystyle+\frac{C_{Q,\mathrm{wt}}}{\sqrt{1-\sqrt{\gamma}}}H_{\nu}(\widehat{w},w^{\pi})

Explicit choices for CQ,wtC_{Q,\mathrm{wt}} and CQ,valC_{Q,\mathrm{val}} are given in Appendix L.1.3. The bound in Theorem S5 consists of the best-candidate error, a Hellinger error for the fitted occupancy ratio, and a validation term of order log⁡(12​K/δ)/(n​gb)/(1−γ)\sqrt{\log(12K/\delta)/(ng_{b})}/(1-\sqrt{\gamma}). Thus, temporal dependence enters through the effective sample size n​gbng_{b}, while the class size enters only logarithmically. For fixed γ\gamma and envelope constants, the validation term vanishes whenever log⁡K=o⁡(n​gb)\log K=o(ng_{b}). Consistency follows when the best-candidate error and Hellinger weight error also vanish. If w^=wπ\widehat{w}=w^{\pi}, the weight-error term is identically zero.

A plug-in value-error bound also holds. Since dπ,γ≥(1−γ)​d0d_{\pi,\gamma}\geq(1-\gamma)d_{0}, we have cconc:=‖d​d0/d​dπ,γ‖∞≤(1−γ)−1c_{\mathrm{conc}}:=\|\mathrm{d}d_{0}/\mathrm{d}d_{\pi,\gamma}\|_{\infty}\leq(1-\gamma)^{-1}, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives |𝔼d0​[Qi^Q​(X)]−Vπ|≤cconc​‖Qi^Q−Qπ‖2,dπ,γ|\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[Q_{\widehat{i}_{Q}}(X)]-V^{\pi}|\leq\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{conc}}}\,\|Q_{\widehat{i}_{Q}}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,d_{\pi,\gamma}}.

The unweighted selector avoids occupancy-ratio estimation but instead requires coercivity (Condition A2) under the offline distribution ν\nu.

    Independent bounded fitted weights. The QQ-validation fold is independent of all data used to construct w^\widehat{w} and the candidates. Conditional on these fitting data, the validation process follows the setup of Section 2.1 and satisfies Condition A1.

Appendix D Joint PBV selection and doubly robust OPE

This appendix applies the two-stage procedure in Algorithm 1 to doubly robust OPE. Its first stage selects an occupancy-ratio candidate, and its second stage uses that ratio to select a QQ-function candidate on the same validation fold. The selected nuisances are then evaluated using a doubly robust estimator on an evaluation fold.

For the joint guarantee in Theorem 5.2, we additionally assume Conditions B1–B3 and either exact d0d_{0} moments or Condition C2 with m=nm=n.

Let the candidates Q1,…,QKQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{K} and w1,…,wMw_{1},\ldots,w_{M} be fitted on a training sample. Let 𝒟sel\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sel}} denote the transition fold shared by the two selection stages, and let 𝒟V\mathcal{D}_{V} denote the evaluation fold, which may equal 𝒟sel\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sel}}. Let 𝒟0,sel\mathcal{D}_{0,\mathrm{sel}} and 𝒟0,V\mathcal{D}_{0,V} denote the corresponding initial-distribution samples when those moments are evaluated empirically.

Let ℙn,V\mathbb{P}_{n,V} denote the empirical average over the evaluation transition fold, and let ℙn,0,V\mathbb{P}_{n,0,V} denote the empirical average over 𝒟0,V\mathcal{D}_{0,V}. The estimator returned by Algorithm S2 is the doubly robust estimator (Jiang and Li, 2016; Kallus and Uehara, 2020):

V^DR:=ℙn,0,V​Q^+11−γ​ℙn,V​[w^​(X)​{R+γ⁡(π​Q^)​(S′)−Q^​(X)}].\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{DR}}:=\mathbb{P}_{n,0,V}\widehat{Q}+\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{P}_{n,V}\!\left[\widehat{w}(X)\{R+\gamma(\pi\widehat{Q})(S^{\prime})-\widehat{Q}(X)\}\right]. (S13)

The following conditions are imposed for the end-to-end analysis.

  1. (D1)

    Validation laws. Each transition fold follows the stationary validation setup of Section 2.1, has invariant distribution ν\nu, and has spectral gap at least gbg_{b}. Each empirical initial-distribution sample consists of independent draws from d0d_{0}.

  2. (D2)

    Selector regularity. Conditions B1, B2, B3, and A3 hold on the selection fold, with constants HQ,GQ,σQ,CwH_{Q},G_{Q},\sigma_{Q},C_{w}, and w¯\overline{w} as defined there.

  3. (D3)

    Initial-value evaluation. Either 𝔼d0​[Qi​(X)]\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[Q_{i}(X)] is known exactly for every candidate, or there is a finite constant σQ,0>0\sigma_{Q,0}>0 such that

    max1≤i≤K⁡𝔼d0​exp​{|Qi​(X0)−𝔼d0​Qi|σQ,0}≤2.\max_{1\leq i\leq K}\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}\exp\left\{\frac{|Q_{i}(X_{0})-\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}Q_{i}|}{\sigma_{Q,0}}\right\}\leq 2.

    When the initial-state expectations under d0d_{0} are evaluated exactly, set σQ,0:=0\sigma_{Q,0}:=0 and interpret ℙn,0,V​Q^\mathbb{P}_{n,0,V}\widehat{Q} in (S13) as 𝔼d0​[Q^​(X)]\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[\widehat{Q}(X)].

The finite candidate classes permit a uniform analysis of both PBV stages and the final estimator, including when the selection and evaluation folds coincide. For the selected ratio, Condition B4 holds by Condition A3.

For the statement below, let

Run Algorithm S2 and suppose Conditions D1–D3 hold. Then, conditional on the training sample, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

(S14)

Here ≲\lesssim suppresses only universal constants and the fixed structural constants in Conditions D2–D3.

The first two terms come from the second-order nuisance remainder. The selection and evaluation samples may coincide.

Appendix E Pairwise validation for projected QQ-functions and occupancy weights

We extend the selectors in Section 4 to the weighted Bellman projection and Bellman–Riesz problems of van der Laan et al. (2025, Section 4 and Appendix G). Each candidate consists of the two functions returned by a minimax fit. Validation uses candidate differences as critics and requires only held-out moments. The working space and projection weight are fixed across candidates.

E.1.  Projected Bellman solutions

Appendix F Pairwise validation for soft optimal control

We extend PBV to KL-regularized optimal control using occupancy weighting and temperature annealing, building on van der Laan and Kallus (2025a). We first bound the error of the selected candidate at a fixed temperature when the initializer and candidate library lie near the soft optimal QQ-function. We then lower the temperature in stages, using the candidate selected by PBV at each stage to initialize the next. Under the stated conditions on candidate accuracy, validation sample sizes, and temperature decreases, this procedure can start from any bounded initializer at a sufficiently high temperature.

F.1.  The soft Bellman operator

Consider a discounted MDP with state space 𝒮\mathcal{S}, finite action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}, transition kernel PP, discount factor γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), and rewards satisfying |R|≤Rmax|R|\leq R_{\max}. Write r(s,a):=𝔼[R∣S=s,A=a]r(s,a):=\mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s,A=a] and X=(S,A)X=(S,A). Fix a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with Lref:=sups,alog⁡{1/πref​(a∣s)}<∞L_{\mathrm{ref}}:=\sup_{s,a}\log\{1/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)\}<\infty. For temperature τ>0\tau>0 and bounded QQ, define the soft state value and its Gibbs policy by

Vτ,Q​(s)\displaystyle V_{\tau,Q}(s) :=τ​log​∑a∈𝒜πref​(a∣s)​eQ⁡(s,a)/τ,\displaystyle:=\tau\log\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)e^{Q(s,a)/\tau}, (S36)
πτ,Q​(a∣s)\displaystyle\pi_{\tau,Q}(a\mid s) :=πref​(a∣s)​exp⁡{[Q⁡(s,a)−Vτ,Q​(s)]/τ}.\displaystyle:=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)\exp\{[Q(s,a)-V_{\tau,Q}(s)]/\tau\}.

The Gibbs policy maximizes expected QQ minus τ\tau times its KL divergence from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The soft Bellman operator and residual map are

(ℬτQ)(s,a):=r(s,a)+γ𝔼[Vτ,Q(S′)∣S=s,A=a],Fτ(Q):=Q−ℬτQ.(\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q)(s,a):=r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}[V_{\tau,Q}(S^{\prime})\mid S=s,A=a],\hskip 18.49988ptF_{\tau}(Q):=Q-\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q. (S37)

The operator satisfies ‖ℬτ​Q−ℬτ​Q′‖∞≤γ​‖Q−Q′‖∞\|\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q-\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q-Q^{\prime}\|_{\infty} and has a unique bounded fixed point Qτ⋆=ℬτ​Qτ⋆Q_{\tau}^{\star}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q_{\tau}^{\star}, with ‖Qτ⋆‖∞≤Rmax/(1−γ)\|Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq R_{\max}/(1-\gamma). For a policy π\pi, let (Pπh)(s,a):=𝔼[∑a′π(a′∣S′)h(S′,a′)∣s,a](P_{\pi}h)(s,a):=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{a^{\prime}}\pi(a^{\prime}\mid S^{\prime})h(S^{\prime},a^{\prime})\mid s,a]. The derivative of the soft Bellman operator is

D​ℬτ​(Q)​[h]=γ​Pπτ,Q​h.D\mathcal{B}_{\tau}(Q)[h]=\gamma P_{\pi_{\tau,Q}}h. (S38)

These properties follow from the log-partition representation; see van der Laan and Kallus (2025a, Section 2 and Lemma S3) for proofs.

F.2.  A fixed temperature and warm start

Fix a temperature τ\tau, a bounded initializer Q¯\bar{Q} with ‖Q¯−Qτ⋆‖∞≤rloc\|\bar{Q}-Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq r_{\mathrm{loc}} for some rloc>0r_{\mathrm{loc}}>0, and an initial state–action distribution d0d_{0}. Let π¯:=πτ,Q¯\bar{\pi}:=\pi_{\tau,\bar{Q}} and let μ\mu be its normalized discounted occupancy measure:

μ:=dπ¯,γ:=(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​d0​Pπ¯t,μ=(1−γ)​d0+γ​μ​Pπ¯.\mu:=d_{\bar{\pi},\gamma}:=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}d_{0}P_{\bar{\pi}}^{t},\hskip 18.49988pt\mu=(1-\gamma)d_{0}+\gamma\mu P_{\bar{\pi}}. (S39)

The adjoint Bellman equation in (S39) gives contraction of γ​Pπ¯\gamma P_{\bar{\pi}} in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu); see van der Laan and Kallus (2025a, Lemma S2).

Proposition S16 (Local contraction and coercivity).

For bounded Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime} satisfying max⁡{‖Q−Q¯‖∞,‖Q′−Q¯‖∞}≤rloc\max\{\|Q-\bar{Q}\|_{\infty},\|Q^{\prime}-\bar{Q}\|_{\infty}\}\leq r_{\mathrm{loc}}, set L:=γ​erloc/τL:=\sqrt{\gamma}\,e^{r_{\mathrm{loc}}/\tau}. Then

‖ℬτ​Q−ℬτ​Q′‖2,μ\displaystyle\|\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q-\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q^{\prime}\|_{2,\mu} ≤L​‖Q−Q′‖2,μ,\displaystyle\leq L\|Q-Q^{\prime}\|_{2,\mu}, (S40)
⟨Q−Q′,Fτ​(Q)−Fτ​(Q′)⟩μ\displaystyle\langle Q-Q^{\prime},F_{\tau}(Q)-F_{\tau}(Q^{\prime})\rangle_{\mu} ≥(1−L)​‖Q−Q′‖2,μ2.\displaystyle\geq(1-L)\|Q-Q^{\prime}\|_{2,\mu}^{2}. (S41)

In particular, the coercivity constant is positive when rloc<τ2​log⁡(1/γ)r_{\mathrm{loc}}<\frac{\tau}{2}\log(1/\gamma).

F.3.  Pairwise validation at a fixed temperature

Condition on the training data and use the temperature τ\tau, initializer Q¯\bar{Q}, and occupancy measure μ\mu from (S39). Assume μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu and set ω:=d​μ/d​ν\omega:=\mathrm{d}\mu/\mathrm{d}\nu. Let Q1,…,QKQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{K} be fitted candidates. Let ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} average over held-out transitions {(Xt,Rt,St′)}t=1n\{(X_{t},R_{t},S_{t}^{\prime})\}_{t=1}^{n}, where XtX_{t} has marginal law ν\nu. For hi​j:=Qi−Qjh_{ij}:=Q_{i}-Q_{j}, define

ℳ^i​jτ\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{ij}^{\tau} :=|ℙn​[ω⁡(X)​hi​j​(X)​{Qi​(X)−R−γ​Vτ,Qi​(S′)}]|\displaystyle:=\left|\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[\omega(X)h_{ij}(X)\{Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma V_{\tau,Q_{i}}(S^{\prime})\}\right]\right| (S42)
−14​|ℙn​[ω⁡(X)​hi​j​(X)​{hi​j​(X)−γ⁡(Vτ,Qi−Vτ,Qj)​(S′)}]|,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\left|\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[\omega(X)h_{ij}(X)\{h_{ij}(X)-\gamma(V_{\tau,Q_{i}}-V_{\tau,Q_{j}})(S^{\prime})\}\right]\right|,
i^τ\displaystyle\widehat{i}_{\tau} :=min⁡arg​mini∈[K]⁡maxj∈[K]​ℳ^ijτ.\displaystyle:=\min\argmin_{i\in[K]}\max_{j\in[K]}\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{ij}^{\tau}.

The first moment tests the soft Bellman equation against the candidate difference. The penalty uses the difference between the two soft Bellman residuals, so both terms are computed from the same fitted functions and held-out transitions.

Let k⋆∈arg​mini∈[K]⁡‖Qi−Qτ⋆‖2,μk^{\star}\in\argmin_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}-Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{2,\mu}. We impose the following conditions, conditional on training.

  1. (SC1)

    Validation process. The validation sample is independent of the data used to construct the candidates, temperature, and weight. It follows the stationary validation setup of Section 2.1 and satisfies Condition A1 with spectral gap gbg_{b}.

  2. (SC2)

    Bounded candidates and weight. There are finite constants B,WB,W such that maxi∈[K]⁡‖Qi‖∞≤B\max_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq B and 0≤ω≤W0\leq\omega\leq W, ν\nu-almost surely.

  3. (SC3)

    Warm start and local library. For a radius 0<rloc<τ2​log⁡(1/γ)0<r_{\mathrm{loc}}<\frac{\tau}{2}\log(1/\gamma),

    ‖Q¯−Qτ⋆‖∞≤rloc,maxi∈[K]⁡‖Qi−Q¯‖∞≤rloc.\|\bar{Q}-Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq r_{\mathrm{loc}},\hskip 18.49988pt\max_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}-\bar{Q}\|_{\infty}\leq r_{\mathrm{loc}}.
Theorem S17 (Oracle bound at a fixed temperature).

Under Conditions SC1–SC3, set L:=γ​erloc/τ<1L:=\sqrt{\gamma}e^{r_{\mathrm{loc}}/\tau}<1. There is a finite constant CC, depending only on B,W,RmaxB,W,R_{\max} and γ\gamma, such that, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with conditional probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

‖Qi^τ−Qτ⋆‖2,μ≤3+L1−L​mini∈[K]​‖Qi−Qτ⋆‖2,μ+C1−L​log⁡(2​K/δ)n​gb.\|Q_{\widehat{i}_{\tau}}-Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{2,\mu}\leq\frac{3+L}{1-L}\min_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}-Q_{\tau}^{\star}\|_{2,\mu}+\frac{C}{1-L}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2K/\delta)}{ng_{b}}}. (S43)

F.4.  Stagewise validation and temperature annealing

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), temperatures τ0>⋯>τJ>0\tau_{0}>\cdots>\tau_{J}>0, and a constant 0<c<12​log⁡(1/γ)0<c<\frac{1}{2}\log(1/\gamma). At stage jj, use an initializer Q¯j\bar{Q}_{j}, its policy πτj,Q¯j\pi_{\tau_{j},\bar{Q}_{j}}, and the occupancy measure μj:=dπτj,Q¯j,γ\mu_{j}:=d_{\pi_{\tau_{j},\bar{Q}_{j}},\gamma}. Keep this measure and temperature fixed while selecting among Qj,1,…,Qj,KjQ_{j,1},\ldots,Q_{j,K_{j}}, and require

maxi∈[Kj]⁡‖Qj,i−Q¯j‖∞≤c​τj.\max_{i\in[K_{j}]}\|Q_{j,i}-\bar{Q}_{j}\|_{\infty}\leq c\tau_{j}. (S44)

Write L0:=γ​ec<1L_{0}:=\sqrt{\gamma}e^{c}<1 and let

εj:=3+L01−L0​mini∈[Kj]​‖Qj,i−Qτj⋆‖2,μj+C1−L0​log⁡{2​Kj​(J+1)/δ}nj​gb,\varepsilon_{j}:=\frac{3+L_{0}}{1-L_{0}}\min_{i\in[K_{j}]}\|Q_{j,i}-Q_{\tau_{j}}^{\star}\|_{2,\mu_{j}}+\frac{C}{1-L_{0}}\sqrt{\frac{\log\{2K_{j}(J+1)/\delta\}}{n_{j}g_{b}}}, (S45)

where njn_{j} is the validation sample size at stage jj and CC is the constant from Theorem S17. To transfer these bounds between temperatures, suppose there are C0<∞C_{0}<\infty and α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1] such that

∥Qj,i−Qτj⋆∥∞≤C0∥Qj,i−Qτj⋆∥2,d0α(i∈[Kj], 0≤j≤J).\|Q_{j,i}-Q_{\tau_{j}}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{0}\|Q_{j,i}-Q_{\tau_{j}}^{\star}\|_{2,d_{0}}^{\alpha}\hskip 18.49988pt(i\in[K_{j}],\ 0\leq j\leq J). (S46)

‖Qτ⋆−Qτ′⋆‖∞≤γ​Lref1−γ​|τ−τ′|.\|Q_{\tau}^{\star}-Q_{\tau^{\prime}}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\gamma L_{\mathrm{ref}}}{1-\gamma}|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|. (S47)

  1. (AN1)

Theorem S18 (PBV under temperature annealing).

Under Conditions SC1–SC2 at every stage, the library and interpolation bounds (S44) and (S46), and Conditions AN1–AN2, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously for 0≤j≤J0\leq j\leq J,

‖Q¯j−Qτj⋆‖∞≤c​τj,‖Q^j−Qτj⋆‖2,μj≤εj,\|\bar{Q}_{j}-Q_{\tau_{j}}^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq c\tau_{j},\hskip 18.49988pt\|\widehat{Q}_{j}-Q_{\tau_{j}}^{\star}\|_{2,\mu_{j}}\leq\varepsilon_{j}, (S49)

where εj\varepsilon_{j} is defined in (S45).

Proof of Proposition S16.

Let h:=Q−Q′h:=Q-Q^{\prime} and Qt:=Q′+t​hQ_{t}:=Q^{\prime}+th for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. The segment satisfies ‖Qt−Q¯‖∞≤rloc\|Q_{t}-\bar{Q}\|_{\infty}\leq r_{\mathrm{loc}}. μ​Pπτ,Qt≤e2​rloc/τ​μ​Pπ¯≤γ−1​e2​rloc/τ​μ.\mu P_{\pi_{\tau,Q_{t}}}\leq e^{2r_{\mathrm{loc}}/\tau}\mu P_{\bar{\pi}}\leq\gamma^{-1}e^{2r_{\mathrm{loc}}/\tau}\mu.

‖ℬτ​Q−ℬτ​Q′‖2,μ≤∫01‖γ​Pπτ,Qt​h‖2,μ​𝑑t≤L​‖h‖2,μ,\|\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q-\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q^{\prime}\|_{2,\mu}\leq\int_{0}^{1}\|\gamma P_{\pi_{\tau,Q_{t}}}h\|_{2,\mu}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq L\|h\|_{2,\mu},

⟨h,Fτ​(Q)−Fτ​(Q′)⟩μ=‖h‖2,μ2−⟨h,ℬτ​Q−ℬτ​Q′⟩μ≥(1−L)​‖h‖2,μ2,\langle h,F_{\tau}(Q)-F_{\tau}(Q^{\prime})\rangle_{\mu}=\|h\|_{2,\mu}^{2}-\langle h,\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q-\mathcal{B}_{\tau}Q^{\prime}\rangle_{\mu}\geq(1-L)\|h\|_{2,\mu}^{2},

on this event. The error bound in that theorem is εj\varepsilon_{j} as defined in (S45).
