Appendix G QQ-function selection: experimental details and additional results

This appendix gives the protocols and additional results for the benchmark comparisons and controlled-overlap studies in Section 6. Occupancy-ratio fitting and its direct evaluation are described separately in Appendix H.

G.1.  Benchmark designs and candidate classes

Released LSTD-Tournament benchmark.

The four model-free Hopper panels vary gravity or transition noise under the original and poor-coverage logging conditions. Each panel contains ten target-policy checkpoints evaluated under three environment settings, giving 120 cases. The model-based gravity and noise panels contain six targets under three settings each, giving 36 cases. We use the released offline transitions, candidate predictions, and policy-value caches. Model-free classes contain 15 simulator-induced QQ-functions; model-based classes contain five candidate models, each inducing a QQ-function and value estimate. Simulator variation controls candidate errors without training FQE; the subgrid experiments vary candidate misspecification. We use new paired bootstrap draws. We compare both LSTD-Tournament variants and squared TD error with our selectors.

DeepOPE/D4RL.

We use all eleven target policies for each of HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, and Ant, with random, medium, medium-replay, medium-expert, and expert D4RL-v2 datasets. The resulting 4×5×11=2204\times 5\times 11=220 cases each use 60 FQE candidates. Four SiLU architectures—two hidden layers of width 64, 128, or 256, and one hidden layer of width 64—are crossed with learning rates 10−410^{-4}, 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, and 10−310^{-3}. Five checkpoints, after 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 fitted-Q iterations, give 60 candidates. Each iteration uses 20 AdamW updates with batch size 512, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and Huber loss. Inputs are standardized, and the target network is updated after each iteration. Fits use γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 without early stopping. Training and validation splits preserve complete trajectories. Each nominal block contains 51,200 transitions. For HalfCheetah and Walker2d medium-replay, the available data cannot supply two disjoint blocks of this size: we first form disjoint trajectory pools and complete each block by resampling whole trajectories within its own pool, retaining at least 90% distinct source transitions. For stochastic targets, QQ-selection predictions average eight next-action draws; reset-value evaluation uses 32 action draws.

Controlled-overlap DeepOPE.

For each DeepOPE environment, the logging policy independently draws one of the eleven benchmark policies uniformly at the start of each trajectory and follows it until termination. Every component is evaluated as a target, giving 44 environment–target cases. Five independent ratio-data replicates are used per case, while the fitted QQ-class and its validation pool remain fixed. Ratio training and validation each use at least 51,200 transitions, with at least three trajectories from every policy component in each split. These samples are independent of the QQ-validation sample. The mixture is uniform over trajectory starts; pooling complete trajectories need not give equal transition mass to each component.

G.2.  Selection criteria

We use unweighted PBV and IW-PBV as defined in Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1. IW-PBV’s T=5T=5 FORE weights are held fixed during QQ-function selection (Appendix H). We also report T=2T=2 in Figure 1, keeping the selected ratios fixed.

For LSTD-Tournament, write εi=Qi​(X)−R−γ​C​(π​Qi)​(S′)\varepsilon_{i}=Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma C(\pi Q_{i})(S^{\prime}), where CC is the continuation indicator. The unnormalized variant minimizes

maxj∈[M]⁡|ℙn​[Qj​εi]|.\max_{j\in[M]}|\mathbb{P}_{n}[Q_{j}\varepsilon_{i}]|.

The normalized-difference variant minimizes

max⁡{|ℙn​[Qi​εi]|σ^n​(Qi),maxj≠i⁡|ℙn​[(Qi−Qj)​εi]|σ^n​(Qi−Qj)},σ^n​(f)2=ℙn​[(f−ℙn​f)2].\max\left\{\frac{|\mathbb{P}_{n}[Q_{i}\varepsilon_{i}]|}{\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(Q_{i})},\;\max_{j\neq i}\frac{|\mathbb{P}_{n}[(Q_{i}-Q_{j})\varepsilon_{i}]|}{\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(Q_{i}-Q_{j})}\right\},\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(f)^{2}=\mathbb{P}_{n}[(f-\mathbb{P}_{n}f)^{2}].

The variance uses divisor nn. A zero standard deviation for any required critic makes the criterion undefined; ties are broken by candidate order. Squared TD error minimizes ℙn​[εi2]\mathbb{P}_{n}[\varepsilon_{i}^{2}]. Both PBV criteria use absolute empirical moments and absolute empirical Bellman energies. The zero function is included as a comparator and cannot be selected. All selectors use identical candidate predictions and validation draws. DeepOPE IW-PBV treats scores within 10−1210^{-12} of the minimum as ties; Hopper IW-PBV uses exact minima.

G.3.  Evaluation metrics

Absolute policy-value error is |V^−Vπ||\widehat{V}-V^{\pi}|, where V^\widehat{V} is the selected candidate’s estimated policy value. For learned candidates, the estimated reset value averages Q^​(S0,A0)\widehat{Q}(S_{0},A_{0}) over 51,200 reset-state draws, integrating target actions as above. Reference values come from the released Hopper caches and, for DeepOPE, from 1,024 target-policy trajectories of horizon at most 1,000.

Following Fu et al. (2021), we normalize true and estimated DeepOPE policy values using the minimum and maximum reference policy values across each environment’s eleven target policies. Absolute errors are thus divided by this range, and initial-state squared errors by its square before pooling. The reference policy values use the same discount, γ=0.99\gamma=0.99, as FQE. Each environment’s range is shared across dataset qualities, full and controlled-overlap studies, methods, validation sample sizes, and candidate counts. Hopper benchmark errors use original return units. The per-environment DeepOPE curves use the same normalization as the aggregate results. Validation resamples, ratio-data replicates, and candidate orders are averaged within each case before cases receive equal weight.

Initial-state value RMSE.

Let v^​(s)=(π​Q^)​(s)\widehat{v}(s)=(\pi\widehat{Q})(s) and let vHπ​(s)v_{H}^{\pi}(s) be the expected discounted return from ss over horizon HH, with zero rewards after termination. We use H=1,024H=1{,}024 for Hopper and H=1,000H=1{,}000 for DeepOPE. For each of N0=1,024N_{0}=1{,}024 reset states S0​jS_{0j}, draw two independent initial actions A0​j(k)∼π(⋅∣S0​j)A_{0j}^{(k)}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid S_{0j}) and two conditionally independent target-policy continuations Gj(k)G_{j}^{(k)}, k=1,2k=1,2. The estimator

ℰ^v,0​(Q^)=1N0​∑j=1N0∏k=12{Q^​(S0​j,A0​j(k))−Gj(k)}\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{v,0}(\widehat{Q})=\frac{1}{N_{0}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{0}}\prod_{k=1}^{2}\{\widehat{Q}(S_{0j},A_{0j}^{(k)})-G_{j}^{(k)}\}

is unbiased for the mean squared state-value error of v^\widehat{v} relative to vHπv_{H}^{\pi} over the reset-state distribution, conditional on the fitted candidate. Independent initial actions ensure that this targets state-value error for stochastic policies. Reusing one initial action would instead target action-value error. For the simulator-defined Hopper candidates, each candidate prediction is replaced by a return in the candidate environment from the same reset state. Candidate and reference environments share random numbers within each branch; the two branches remain independent. Candidate simulations are reused only after checking identical candidate and target-policy parameters. DeepOPE references are shared across dataset qualities for each environment–target pair. RMSE is the square root after pooling the estimated squared errors across selections and cases, rather than the mean of case-level square roots.

G.4.  Validation draws and uncertainty

The released Hopper and full DeepOPE comparisons use nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200. We also report controlled-overlap DeepOPE at nQ=51,200n_{Q}=51{,}200. Released Hopper uses 96 paired transition bootstrap draws per case in both the model-free and model-based settings. Its model-free sample-size curves use nested draws at nQ∈{8,464,920,1376,1832,2288,2744,3200}n_{Q}\in\{8,464,920,1376,1832,2288,2744,3200\}. DeepOPE uses 96 complete-trajectory bootstrap draws at each nominal size. The full and controlled-overlap DeepOPE grid is nQ∈{3,200,6,400,12,800,25,600,51,200}n_{Q}\in\{3{,}200,6{,}400,12{,}800,25{,}600,51{,}200\}. Whole-trajectory sampling can exceed the nominal size. Reference values and evaluation losses are used only after selection; all methods use the same validation draws.

Table S1 reports 95% intervals from 10,000 bootstrap draws over condition–truth groups for Hopper and environment–dataset groups for DeepOPE, after averaging validation resamples, ratio-data replicates, and candidate orders within cases. Methods remain paired in every draw. Controlled-overlap Hopper uses its six perturbation–truth groups. Controlled-overlap DeepOPE instead resamples its four environments, averaging the five ratio-data replicates within each target case first. For RMSE differences, each resampled mean squared error is square-rooted before taking the difference. The ranges of reference policy values remain fixed during resampling. These intervals condition on the fitted candidate libraries and saved Monte Carlo reference values. Validation resamples are not independent training replications; the controlled-overlap DeepOPE study has five independent ratio-data replicates per target, whereas the original benchmarks have one fitted ratio library per case.

G.5.  Candidate counts

The 15-candidate class contains the five checkpoints from each two-layer architecture at learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. The 30-, 45-, and 60-candidate classes add complete training runs from the remaining architecture–rate pairs, using 20 fixed nested orders shared by all methods and cases. The fitted functions, target-action draws, validation resamples, and occupancy weights are shared across candidate counts. Selections are fixed before reference returns or candidate evaluation losses are accessed.

G.6.  Zero comparator

We repeat the PBV and IW-PBV comparisons with and without the zero comparator, holding fitted candidates, selected occupancy ratios, validation draws, and tie rules fixed. Zero is never selectable. Table S2 uses the benchmark groups and validation sample size of Table 1; Figure S3 uses the cases and sample sizes of Figure 1. Including zero substantially reduces both errors on the poor-coverage model-free Hopper grid. Changes are small on the main model-free and model-based Hopper grids and on full DeepOPE; the controlled-overlap curves are nearly unchanged.

G.7.  Critic penalty

We ablate only the QQ-selection penalty, changing its coefficient from 1/41/4 to zero. Fitted candidates, selected occupancy weights, validation draws, candidate orders, and tie rules are fixed; zero remains a comparator and is never selectable. A-PBV ratio selection is unchanged. Table S3 reports this exploratory matched comparison at nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200. Selections are frozen before evaluation losses are accessed.

Removing the penalty increases mean absolute policy-value error on all three released Hopper grids and on controlled-overlap DeepOPE for all three selectors. It slightly reduces both errors on full DeepOPE and improves unweighted PBV on controlled-overlap Hopper. On controlled-overlap DeepOPE, removing the IW-PBV penalty increases value error while slightly reducing initial-state value RMSE. Most released-Hopper paired intervals contain zero.

G.8.  Full DeepOPE on D4RL datasets

Table S4 reports all 220 D4RL environment–dataset–target cases with 60 FQE candidates. Aggregate errors are similar across the PBV and LSTD-Tournament variants, with slightly lower errors for unnormalized LSTD-Tournament at both validation sample sizes. The mean value errors of the PBV and LSTD-Tournament variants are close in HalfCheetah and Ant. In Hopper, unnormalized LSTD-Tournament has lower mean value error than both temperatures of IW-PBV; in Walker2d, T=2T=2 gives lower mean value error than both LSTD-Tournament variants at every displayed sample size.

G.9.  Results on the released Hopper benchmark grids

Figures S5–S8 use the benchmark conditions of Figures 3–5 and 9 of Liu et al. (2025), comparing unweighted PBV and IW-PBV with both LSTD-Tournament variants. The main model-free grids contain 60 cases; the poor-coverage counterparts contain another 60. The five-candidate model-based grids contain 36 cases. We show absolute value error and initial-state value RMSE on the original return scale. The plots report our paired reevaluation of the released candidates. Each curve first averages validation resamples within each target and then averages across targets; RMSE takes the square root after averaging squared errors. The fitted candidates and released Monte Carlo reference values remain fixed. Paired uncertainty for the aggregate comparisons is reported in Table S1. Among the two LSTD-Tournament variants, the normalized variant has lower aggregate errors on the model-based Hopper grids, whereas unnormalized LSTD-Tournament has lower errors on the main and poor-coverage model-free grids (Table 1).

The subgrid experiments reuse the released candidate predictions. For the gap experiments, the true noise-grid model is indexed by 7, and the candidates have indices {7−k,7,7+k}\{7-k,7,7+k\}, k=1,…,7k=1,\ldots,7. For misspecification, the true model is indexed by 0 and the candidate set is {k,…,k+4}\{k,\ldots,k+4\}, k=0,…,10k=0,\ldots,10. These panels average ten targets and 32 paired resamples per subset, with nQ=2,048n_{Q}=2{,}048 for gaps and 3,2003{,}200 for misspecification. The coverage panel uses the gravity-grid model indexed by 0, target policy 8, eight target-data fractions, and 256 paired resamples at nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200. The choice of policy 8 follows the released implementation and Table 1 of Liu et al. (2025). For IW-PBV, fresh auxiliary background and target-policy rollouts are mixed in the same proportions. The background uses the reconstructed deterministic actor, without added action noise. Ratio training and validation each use 3,200 transitions, with the same 56-candidate FORE class, A-PBV selection, and 1/51/5 tempering. The original QQ-validation draws are retained. Because the original background checkpoints are unavailable, IW-PBV uses additional data from reconstructed policies; Appendix H details this limitation.

G.10.  Controlled-overlap Hopper

The controlled-overlap Hopper study uses the same 60-candidate FQE construction as DeepOPE, with independent training and validation samples of at least 51,200 transitions. The logging policy draws one of the ten benchmark policies uniformly at the start of each trajectory and follows it until termination. Ten targets in each of two perturbation grids and three true environments give 60 cases. Thus, these candidates and data are distinct from the released simulator-induced QQ-classes in the LSTD-Tournament comparison. Each case uses five fixed permutations of its 51,200-transition validation pool, with nested subsamples; these are validation draws, not independent FQE refits. Occupancy weights are held fixed across candidate counts. Table S5 reports both endpoints of the validation grid. At T=5T=5, IW-PBV has lower mean absolute policy-value error and initial-state value RMSE than unweighted PBV and both LSTD-Tournament variants at both sample sizes. The T=5T=5 errors are lower than those at T=2T=2 for nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200; this ordering reverses at nQ=51,200n_{Q}=51{,}200.

Appendix H Occupancy-ratio selection experiments

We compare A-PBV with our adjoint LSTD extension on direct occupancy-ratio errors and on the resulting IW-PBV selections. The direct comparison uses FORE, DualDICE, and their combined candidate library; the downstream comparison uses five benchmark groups. A-PBV gives lower aggregate direct ratio errors across all three libraries, while downstream performance varies across benchmarks. We also examine tempering; the main experiments report the fixed temperatures T=2T=2 and T=5T=5.

H.1.  Ratio fitting, screening, and normalization

Benchmark FORE libraries.

The benchmark ratio libraries contain neural FORE estimators (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026) fitted with AdamW, learning rates 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} and 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and checkpoints after 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, and 1,600 updates. DeepOPE uses one or two hidden layers of width 64, giving 28 candidates. The Hopper extension also includes two-layer networks of widths 32 and 128, giving 56 candidates. Ratio training and validation each use 3,200 transitions for Hopper, 25,600 for full DeepOPE, and at least 51,200 for controlled-overlap DeepOPE. The latter uses five independent data replicates per environment–target pair. In the released 15-candidate Hopper comparisons, ratio predictions outside the known target-action support are set to the prediction floor. The model-based and coverage-mixture extensions use unprojected predictions.

Direct ratio libraries.

FORE uses architectures (64)(64), (64,64)(64,64), (32,32)(32,32), and (128,128)(128,128), with the learning rates and checkpoints above. DualDICE uses architectures (64)(64), (64,64)(64,64), (128,128)(128,128), and (256,256)(256,256); multipliers 0.30.3 and 11 on its default learning rates 10−410^{-4} and 10−310^{-3} for the two networks; and checkpoints at 100, 250, 500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, and 10,000 updates. We use the unchanged continuous-action update from the official Google implementation. FORE and DualDICE use minibatches of 1,024 and 256, respectively.

Screening and normalization.

The screen follows the fitted estimator’s training normalization. Let uju_{j} denote its predictions after flooring the raw output at 10−610^{-6} and applying the training normalization. Using the ratio-training empirical measure ℙn,w\mathbb{P}_{n,w} and the continuation indicator CC, define

cj​(x)=min⁡{uj​(x),50},vj​(x)=(1−γ)​cj​(x)ℙn,w​[cj​(X)​(1−γ​C)].c_{j}(x)=\min\{u_{j}(x),50\},\hskip 18.49988ptv_{j}(x)=\frac{(1-\gamma)c_{j}(x)}{\mathbb{P}_{n,w}[c_{j}(X)(1-\gamma C)]}.

This rescaling enforces the empirical occupancy-mass identity on the training sample. We retain candidate jj if

(ℙn,w​vj)2ℙn,w​vj2≥0.05,\frac{(\mathbb{P}_{n,w}v_{j})^{2}}{\mathbb{P}_{n,w}v_{j}^{2}}\geq 0.05,

and use w~j​(x)=min⁡{vj​(x),50}\widetilde{w}_{j}(x)=\min\{v_{j}(x),50\} for selection and evaluation. The capped candidates are not rescaled before ratio selection. The same transformation applies to current-state, next-target, reset, and QQ-validation predictions. For stochastic DeepOPE targets, ratio validation uses one common target-action draw per next state and reset state, shared by all candidates. The QQ-selection action averages are described in Appendix G.

For downstream weighting, we use wT=w~1/T/ℙn,w​[w~1/T]w_{T}=\widetilde{w}^{1/T}/\mathbb{P}_{n,w}[\widetilde{w}^{1/T}] with T=5T=5 (Sinha et al., 2022). The normalizer is a positive common factor and leaves IW-PBV selections unchanged. The temperature comparison also includes T=1T=1, which uses the untempered ratio, and T=2,3,4T=2,3,4.

Auxiliary data for Hopper.

The unweighted Hopper comparisons reuse the released logging data. IW-PBV additionally uses independently collected ratio-training and validation samples. The poor-coverage behavior checkpoints are absent, so these rollouts use policies reconstructed from the released state–action pairs. For the coverage-mixture panel, we refit FORE using deterministic reconstructed background actors without added action noise, retaining the released QQ-candidates and validation draws. Thus these weighted experiments use an approximation to the original behavior policy.

H.2.  Direct ratio errors

We use a separate 18-case Hopper experiment with gravity and noise perturbations, three perturbation levels, and three target policies. Each case has disjoint training, validation, and evaluation samples of 10,000 transitions each. Three optimizer seeds (17,19,23)(17,19,23) use the same data split. The logging law is the known equal mixture

ν=13​∑ℓ=13dπℓ,γmℓ,mℓ=∫d​dπℓ,γ,\nu=\tfrac{1}{3}\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{d_{\pi_{\ell},\gamma}}{m_{\ell}},\hskip 18.49988ptm_{\ell}=\int\mathrm{d}d_{\pi_{\ell},\gamma},

where dπℓ,γd_{\pi_{\ell},\gamma} is the preterminal discounted occupancy measure. For a component target π\pi, the true ratio is wπ=3​mπ​Pr⁡(component=π∣X)w^{\pi}=3m_{\pi}\Pr(\text{component}=\pi\mid X). The component policies are deterministic: on a unique target action graph, wπ=3​mπw^{\pi}=3m_{\pi}, and off that graph it is zero. All 180,000 evaluation observations have identified graph membership at action tolerance 10−510^{-5}. At 10−410^{-4}, two observations are ambiguous; we retain error bounds for them. An independent sample of 1,024 complete target trajectories per case is used to estimate mπm_{\pi}, with maximum Monte Carlo standard error 0.004570.00457.

We compare three candidate libraries: 56 FORE candidates, 56 DualDICE candidates (Nachum et al., 2019), and their 112-candidate union. Each fitting family varies four architectures, two learning rates, and seven checkpoints (Section H.1). All predictions in this experiment are unprojected. The ESS screen removes 167 of 3,024 fitted FORE candidates and 4 of 3,024 DualDICE candidates, leaving 44–56 and 55–56 candidates per library, respectively. Both selectors are defined in all 54 fitting runs for each library. Our adjoint LSTD extension applies normalized-difference LSTD-Tournament to the adjoint Bellman equation (Appendix P).

We report the unhalved Hellinger distance Hν​(w,wπ)={∫(w−wπ)2​𝑑ν}1/2H_{\nu}(w,w^{\pi})=\{\int(\sqrt{w}-\sqrt{w^{\pi}})^{2}\mathrm{d}\nu\}^{1/2}, ratio RMSE {∫(w−wπ)2​𝑑ν}1/2\{\int(w-w^{\pi})^{2}\mathrm{d}\nu\}^{1/2}, generalized KL from the true ratio to the candidate

∫{wπ​log⁡(wπ/w)−wπ+w}​𝑑ν,\int\{w^{\pi}\log(w^{\pi}/w)-w^{\pi}+w\}\mathrm{d}\nu,

and absolute importance-weighted reward error |𝔼ν​[w​r]−(1−γ)​Vπ||\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[wr]-(1-\gamma)V^{\pi}|. Known component weights are used when averaging evaluation samples. We average risks over optimizer seeds within cases, then over cases; Hellinger distance and ratio RMSE take the square root after averaging. Intervals use 10,000 paired cluster-bootstrap draws over the six groups defined by perturbation type and level, holding the data splits and estimated occupancy masses fixed.

A-PBV has lower aggregate error on all four metrics in each library (Table S6). Its Hellinger differences relative to adjoint LSTD are −0.046-0.046 (95% interval [−0.079,−0.008][-0.079,-0.008]) for FORE, −0.032-0.032 ([−0.048,−0.019][-0.048,-0.019]) for DualDICE, and −0.043-0.043 ([−0.071,−0.006][-0.071,-0.006]) for their union. DualDICE gives the lowest Hellinger distance, ratio RMSE, and reward error under both selectors; FORE gives the lowest generalized KL. Adding FORE candidates to DualDICE does not lower its aggregate errors. Figure S9 shows Hellinger error by perturbation.

The known-ratio construction uses a mixture of normalized discounted occupancies. The released Hopper caches instead pool complete-trajectory transitions, so we use the controlled experiment for direct ratio errors and the benchmark data for downstream QQ-selection errors.

H.3.  Downstream ratio selection and tempering

We compare the two ratio selectors across five benchmark groups at nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200. The QQ-selection rule is IW-PBV throughout; the fitted QQ-candidates, ratio data, ESS screen, cap, and validation draws are shared. Only the ratio selector and temperature vary. All 596 ratio selections are defined for both selectors. These experiments use the benchmark FORE libraries described above. DeepOPE uses the 60-candidate QQ-libraries from the main experiments.

The two ratio selectors give similar aggregate errors on poor-coverage Hopper and full DeepOPE at both temperatures (Table S7). A-PBV has lower mean errors on controlled DeepOPE, and Adjoint LSTD-Tournament on the main model-free and model-based Hopper groups. The paired intervals for the DeepOPE and poor-coverage comparisons include zero. The direct ratio-error advantage of A-PBV therefore does not consistently improve downstream errors.

Figure S10 compares fixed temperatures T=1,2,5T=1,2,5 across the DeepOPE validation sample sizes, holding fitted candidates and A-PBV-selected ratios fixed. Untempered weighting (T=1T=1) gives slightly lower aggregate errors than T=2T=2 and T=5T=5 on full DeepOPE at every displayed sample size. Among the three plotted temperatures, T=5T=5 gives lower errors under controlled overlap at nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200, whereas T=2T=2 gives the lowest mean value error and RMSE at nQ=25,600n_{Q}=25{,}600 and 51,20051{,}200. At the latter sample size, T=2T=2 lowers these errors by 13% and 27% relative to T=5T=5.

At nQ=3,200n_{Q}=3{,}200, however, T=5T=5 has the lowest aggregate errors on all three Hopper groups. Averaging percentage changes equally over the five benchmark groups, untempered A-PBV-selected weights increase mean value error by 49.7%49.7\% (95% cluster-bootstrap interval [35.3%,66.3%][35.3\%,66.3\%]) and initial-state value RMSE by 35.1%35.1\% ([21.2%,47.5%][21.2\%,47.5\%]) relative to T=5T=5. The corresponding increases with Adjoint LSTD-Tournament are 28.4%28.4\% and 20.4%20.4\%. The bootstrap resamples environment/truth groups for Hopper and environments for DeepOPE, with shared draws across related benchmark groups.

Independent validation sample.

We repeated QQ-function selection for the 44 controlled-overlap DeepOPE cases on independently collected mixture trajectories, using a nominal 51,20051{,}200 validation transitions per environment. The fitted candidates, selected ratios, temperatures T=2,5T=2,5, and evaluation reference values were held fixed. All selections on the new sample were saved before evaluation. Table S8 reports the resulting errors. Relative to unweighted PBV, the percentage changes with T=2T=2 are −5.9%-5.9\% for value error (95% interval [−25.5%,45.3%][-25.5\%,45.3\%]) and −8.0%-8.0\% for initial-state value RMSE ([−26.4%,86.4%][-26.4\%,86.4\%]). The paired bootstrap resamples the four environments; negative changes favor IW-PBV. The aggregate gains are smaller than on the original validation pool.

Appendix I On-policy examples for LSTD-Tournament

The three examples in Figure S1 study amplification of moment noise, error in estimating critic standard deviations, and near-collinearity between candidates.

I.1.  Noise amplification

Data-generating process.

We use a continuing Markov decision process with one action and state space [−1,1]5[-1,1]^{5}. The initial state and each subsequent state are independent uniform draws from this cube. Rewards are R=0.1+ξR=0.1+\xi, where ξ∼N⁡(0,0.22)\xi\sim N(0,0.2^{2}) is independent of the states and other rewards. With discount γ=0.9\gamma=0.9, the true value function is Qπ​(s)=1Q^{\pi}(s)=1 and the policy value is Vπ=1V^{\pi}=1. The validation distribution is the stationary distribution of the target policy, so the experiment is on-policy.

Candidates.

The fixed candidate class is 𝒬={Qh:h∈ℋ}\mathcal{Q}=\{Q_{h}:h\in\mathcal{H}\}, where

Qh​(s)=1+exp⁡(−‖s‖22​h2).Q_{h}(s)=1+\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|s\|^{2}}{2h^{2}}\right).

The 200 bandwidths comprise 100 logarithmically spaced values in [10−6,0.1)[10^{-6},0.1) and 100 in [0.1,10][0.1,10]. More precisely,

ℋ={10−6+5​j/100:j=0,…,99}∪{10−1+2​j/99:j=0,…,99}.\mathcal{H}=\{10^{-6+5j/100}:j=0,\ldots,99\}\cup\{10^{-1+2j/99}:j=0,\ldots,99\}.

All candidates take values between one and two.

Selectors.

For validation observations (St,Rt,St′)t=1n(S_{t},R_{t},S_{t}^{\prime})_{t=1}^{n}, write ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} for the empirical average and define

m^h​(f)=ℙn​[f⁡(S)​{Qh​(S)−R−γ​Qh​(S′)}],ℰ^​(f)=ℙn​[f⁡(S)​{f⁡(S)−γ​f​(S′)}].\widehat{m}_{h}(f)=\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[f(S)\{Q_{h}(S)-R-\gamma Q_{h}(S^{\prime})\}\right],\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(f)=\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[f(S)\{f(S)-\gamma f(S^{\prime})\}\right].

Unweighted PBV minimizes

T^hPBV=maxg∈𝒬∪{0}⁡{|m^h​(Qh−g)|−14​|ℰ^​(Qh−g)|}.\widehat{T}_{h}^{\mathrm{PBV}}=\max_{g\in\mathcal{Q}\cup\{0\}}\left\{|\widehat{m}_{h}(Q_{h}-g)|-\tfrac{1}{4}|\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(Q_{h}-g)|\right\}.

Zero is an additional comparator; the selected function belongs to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Unnormalized LSTD-Tournament minimizes

T^hLT=maxg∈𝒬⁡|m^h​(g)|.\widehat{T}_{h}^{\mathrm{LT}}=\max_{g\in\mathcal{Q}}|\widehat{m}_{h}(g)|.

Normalized LSTD-Tournament uses the candidate and difference critics of the published implementation and minimizes

T^hLT,nd=max⁡{|m^h​(Qh)|σ^n​(Qh),maxg∈𝒬∖{Qh}⁡|m^h​(Qh−g)|σ^n​(Qh−g)},\widehat{T}_{h}^{\mathrm{LT,nd}}=\max\left\{\frac{|\widehat{m}_{h}(Q_{h})|}{\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(Q_{h})},\;\max_{g\in\mathcal{Q}\setminus\{Q_{h}\}}\frac{|\widehat{m}_{h}(Q_{h}-g)|}{\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(Q_{h}-g)}\right\},

where σ^n​(f)2=ℙn​[(f−ℙn​f)2]\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(f)^{2}=\mathbb{P}_{n}[(f-\mathbb{P}_{n}f)^{2}]. The L2L^{2}-normalized tournament uses the same candidate and difference critics, replacing each σ^n​(f)\widehat{\sigma}_{n}(f) by {ℙn​f2}1/2\{\mathbb{P}_{n}f^{2}\}^{1/2}. We evaluate normalized scores using rescaled Gaussian bumps and logarithms to avoid numerical underflow. All four selectors use the same observations. Candidate order is randomized once per repetition and shared across methods to resolve ties.

Evaluation.

We generate 500 independent validation datasets of 4,096 transitions and use nested prefixes of sizes n∈{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096}n\in\{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096\}. Errors are evaluated exactly under the uniform initial-state distribution. For gh=Qh−1g_{h}=Q_{h}-1 and p∈{1,2}p\in\{1,2\},

mp​(h):=𝔼⁡[gh​(S)p]={π2​hp​erf⁡(p2​h)}5.m_{p}(h):=\mathbb{E}[g_{h}(S)^{p}]=\left\{\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{h}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{p}}{\sqrt{2}h}\right)\right\}^{5}.

The absolute policy-value error of QhQ_{h} is m1​(h)m_{1}(h), and its initial-state mean squared value error is m2​(h)m_{2}(h). Figure S11 reports the square root of the average m2m_{2} across selected candidates and the average m1m_{1} in its left and right panels, respectively. The 95% intervals use 5,000 bootstrap resamples of the independent datasets, preserving pairing across selectors and validation sizes. Each bootstrap RMSE is computed after averaging squared errors.

I.2.  Standard-deviation estimation error

Data-generating process and candidates.

We use one action, discount γ=0\gamma=0, and independent states S=(X,U,V)S=(X,U,V) with independent coordinates uniform on [−1,1][-1,1]. For h=10−4h=10^{-4}, define

kh(x)=exp{−x2/(2h2)},p=𝔼[kh(X)]=π2herf(12​h),ϵ=p3.k_{h}(x)=\exp\{-x^{2}/(2h^{2})\},\hskip 18.49988ptp=\mathbb{E}[k_{h}(X)]=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,h\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}h}\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\epsilon=p^{3}.

R⁡(S)=Qπ​(S)=p2+ϵ​U+kh​(X).R(S)=Q^{\pi}(S)=\frac{p}{2}+\epsilon U+k_{h}(X).

Q1=Qπ+p2,Qj+1=Qπ+kbj(V),j=1,…,199,Q_{1}=Q^{\pi}+\frac{p}{2},\hskip 18.49988ptQ_{j+1}=Q^{\pi}+k_{b_{j}}(V),\hskip 18.49988ptj=1,\ldots,199,

where bj=14​ 8(j−1)/198b_{j}=\tfrac{1}{4}\,8^{(j-1)/198} gives 199 logarithmically spaced bandwidths from 0.250.25 to 22. The Gaussian perturbations have no constant shift. Their TD residuals are p/2p/2 and kbj​(V)k_{b_{j}}(V), so there is no conditional TD noise. The background term ϵ​U\epsilon U makes empirical critic standard deviations positive almost surely.

Selectors and population standard deviations.

We apply the same unweighted PBV, unnormalized LSTD, and empirical-SD-normalized LSTD criteria to this library. The fourth selector is an oracle control: it retains exactly the empirical moments and critics of the SD-normalized tournament but uses population standard deviations. For independent uniform Z∈[−1,1]Z\in[-1,1], define

M⁡(b)=𝔼⁡[kb​(Z)]=π2​b​erf⁡(12​b),C(b,c)=M((b−2+c−2)−1/2)−M(b)M(c).\begin{gathered}M(b)=\mathbb{E}[k_{b}(Z)]=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,b\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}b}\right),\\ C(b,c)=M\!\left((b^{-2}+c^{-2})^{-1/2}\right)-M(b)M(c).\end{gathered}

Thus vh:=Varν⁡(Qπ)=M⁡(h/2)−p2+ϵ2/3v_{h}:=\operatorname{Var}_{\nu}(Q^{\pi})=M(h/\sqrt{2})-p^{2}+\epsilon^{2}/3, σν​(Q1)2=vh\sigma_{\nu}(Q_{1})^{2}=v_{h}, and Covν⁡(Qi+1,Qj+1)=vh+C⁡(bi,bj)\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu}(Q_{i+1},Q_{j+1})=v_{h}+C(b_{i},b_{j}). Since Q1−Qj+1=p/2−kbj​(V)Q_{1}-Q_{j+1}=p/2-k_{b_{j}}(V), its variance is C⁡(bj,bj)C(b_{j},b_{j}); the remaining difference variances follow from the displayed covariance.

Evaluation.

We use 500 independent datasets, the same nested validation sizes as above, a common randomized candidate order across methods, and 5,000 paired bootstrap resamples. The exact initial-state mean squared errors are p2/4p^{2}/4 for Q1Q_{1} and M⁡(bj/2)M(b_{j}/\sqrt{2}) for Qj+1Q_{j+1}; the absolute policy-value errors are p/2p/2 and M⁡(bj)M(b_{j}), respectively.

I.3.  Near-collinearity

Data-generating process and candidates.

We use one action, discount γ=0\gamma=0, and independent states S=(F,U)S=(F,U), where FF and UU are independent uniform draws from [−3,3][-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3}]. Write G=1+UG=1+U and set A=104A=10^{4}. Rewards are R=A​F+ξR=AF+\xi, with independent ξ∼N⁡(0,0.22)\xi\sim N(0,0.2^{2}), so Qπ​(S)=A​FQ^{\pi}(S)=AF and Vπ=0V^{\pi}=0. The 200 fixed candidates are

Qt​(S)=A​F+t​G,t∈𝒯.Q_{t}(S)=AF+tG,\hskip 18.49988ptt\in\mathcal{T}.

We form 𝒯\mathcal{T} from 200 equally spaced values in [−1,1][-1,1], replacing the positive value closest to zero by zero. All candidates share the large component A​FAF, while Qt−Qs=(t−s)​GQ_{t}-Q_{s}=(t-s)G. Their population standard deviations are σν​(Qt)=A2+t2\sigma_{\nu}(Q_{t})=\sqrt{A^{2}+t^{2}} and σν​(Qt−Qs)=|t−s|\sigma_{\nu}(Q_{t}-Q_{s})=|t-s| for t≠st\neq s. The centered candidate span has spikiness measure 66, and the noise amplification factors are at most 2\sqrt{2}.

Selectors and evaluation.

We apply unweighted PBV and the unnormalized and empirical-SD-normalized LSTD-Tournament criteria defined above. All three use the same observations and randomized candidate order. We use 500 independent datasets, the same nested validation sizes, and 5,000 paired bootstrap resamples as in the other examples. For QtQ_{t}, the exact initial-state mean squared value error is 2​t22t^{2}, and the absolute policy-value error is |t||t|.

Appendix J Shared concentration bounds

The dependence argument used for all three selectors combines Bernstein concentration for bounded additive functionals of a Markov chain with martingale concentration for the centered one-step transition term. Let ℱt:=σ⁡(X1,R1,S1′,…,Xt−1,Rt−1,St−1′,Xt)\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma(X_{1},R_{1},S_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,X_{t-1},R_{t-1},S_{t-1}^{\prime},X_{t}). Under the validation setup, conditional on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, the pair (Rt,St′)(R_{t},S_{t}^{\prime}) follows the MDP reward and transition law given XtX_{t}.

Lemma S19 (Trajectory Bernstein bounds).

Let U1,…,UnU_{1},\ldots,U_{n} be a stationary Markov chain with invariant law μ\mu and transition operator PUP_{U}. Suppose, for some g∈(0,1]g\in(0,1], ‖PU​f‖2,μ≤(1−g)​‖f‖2,μ\|P_{U}f\|_{2,\mu}\leq(1-g)\|f\|_{2,\mu} for every centered real-valued f∈L2​(μ)f\in L^{2}(\mu); alternatively, PUP_{U} is self-adjoint and ⟨f,PU​f⟩μ≤(1−g)​‖f‖2,μ2\langle f,P_{U}f\rangle_{\mu}\leq(1-g)\|f\|_{2,\mu}^{2} for every such ff. Let (ℱt)t=1n+1(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=1}^{n+1} be a filtration such that UtU_{t} is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable and YtY_{t} is ℱt+1\mathcal{F}_{t+1}-measurable. Suppose there is a Markov kernel KYK_{Y}, not depending on tt, such that ℒ⁡(Yt∣ℱt)=KY​(Ut,⋅)\mathcal{L}(Y_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t})=K_{Y}(U_{t},\cdot) for every tt. For u≥1u\geq 1, set rg​(u):=u/(n​g)r_{g}(u):=\sqrt{u/(ng)}.

  1. (i)

    If |Yt|≤B|Y_{t}|\leq B almost surely and 𝔼⁡(Yt2)≤v2\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{2})\leq v^{2}, then, with probability at least 1−6​e−u1-6e^{-u},

    |1n​∑t=1nYt−𝔼​Yt|≤CM​{v​rg​(u)+B​rg​(u)2}.\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}Y_{t}-\mathbb{E}Y_{t}\right|\leq C_{\mathrm{M}}\{vr_{g}(u)+Br_{g}(u)^{2}\}. (S53)
  2. (ii)

    Suppose Yt=a⁡(Ut)​{d⁡(Ut)+ζt}Y_{t}=a(U_{t})\{d(U_{t})+\zeta_{t}\}, where |a|≤B|a|\leq B, |d|≤D|d|\leq D, 𝔼μ​(a2)≤v2\mathbb{E}_{\mu}(a^{2})\leq v^{2}, σ>0\sigma>0, and

    𝔼(ζt∣ℱt)=0,𝔼[exp{|ζt|σ}|ℱt]≤2.\mathbb{E}(\zeta_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t})=0,\hskip 18.49988pt\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.\exp\left\{\frac{|\zeta_{t}|}{\sigma}\right\}\right|\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq 2. (S54)

    Then, with probability at least 1−6​e−u1-6e^{-u},

    |1n​∑t=1nYt−𝔼​Yt|≤CM​(D+σ)​{v​rg​(u)+B​rg​(u)2}.\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}Y_{t}-\mathbb{E}Y_{t}\right|\leq C_{\mathrm{M}}(D+\sigma)\{vr_{g}(u)+Br_{g}(u)^{2}\}. (S55)

Here CM>0C_{\mathrm{M}}>0 is a universal constant.

|1n​∑t=1nf⁡(Ut)|≤C⁡{‖f‖2,μ​un​g+‖f‖∞​un​g}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f(U_{t})\right|\leq C\left\{\|f\|_{2,\mu}\sqrt{\frac{u}{ng}}+\|f\|_{\infty}\frac{u}{ng}\right\} (S56)

Appendix K Proofs for A-PBV

K.1.  Generalized-KL contraction and adjoint residual identities

The following generalized-KL contraction was established in the FORE analysis of van der Laan and Kallus (2026).

Lemma S20 (Generalized-KL contraction of the adjoint update).

Let ww and w~\widetilde{w} be nonnegative integrable functions whose adjoint updates exist as ν\nu-densities. Then

𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥ℬπ∗w~)≤γ𝖣ν(w∥w~),\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}\widetilde{w})\leq\gamma\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|\widetilde{w}), (S59)

whenever the divergence on the right is finite.

Proof of Lemma S20.

Write 𝖣\mathsf{D} for generalized KL between finite nonnegative measures. This divergence is jointly convex and obeys the data-processing inequality for Markov kernels. Let μ=w​ν\mu=w\nu and μ~=w~​ν\widetilde{\mu}=\widetilde{w}\nu. By (2), joint convexity, and data processing,

𝖣ν(ℬπ∗w∥ℬπ∗w~)\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w\|\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}\widetilde{w}) =𝖣⁡((1−γ)​d0+γ​μ​Pπ∥(1−γ)​d0+γ​μ~​Pπ)\displaystyle=\mathsf{D}\!\left((1-\gamma)d_{0}+\gamma\mu P_{\pi}\,\middle\|\,(1-\gamma)d_{0}+\gamma\widetilde{\mu}P_{\pi}\right)
≤(1−γ)𝖣(d0∥d0)+γ𝖣(μPπ∥μ~Pπ)\displaystyle\leq(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}(d_{0}\|d_{0})+\gamma\mathsf{D}(\mu P_{\pi}\|\widetilde{\mu}P_{\pi})
≤γ𝖣(μ∥μ~)=γ𝖣ν(w∥w~),\displaystyle\leq\gamma\mathsf{D}(\mu\|\widetilde{\mu})=\gamma\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|\widetilde{w}),

which is (S59). ∎

Lemma S21 (Generalized-KL three-point identity for the adjoint residual).

Let ww and vv be nonnegative integrable functions that are positive on a common measurable support and vanish ν\nu-almost surely off that support. Set log⁡(w/v)=0\log(w/v)=0 where both functions vanish, and suppose w+:=ℬπ∗​ww^{+}:=\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w exists as a nonnegative ν\nu-density. If every divergence in (S60) is finite, then

𝔼ν[(w−w+)logwv]=𝖣ν(w∥v)−𝖣ν(w+∥v)+𝖣ν(w+∥w).\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[(w-w^{+})\log\frac{w}{v}\right]=\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|v)-\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w^{+}\|v)+\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w^{+}\|w). (S60)

In particular, if v=wπv=w^{\pi}, then

𝒮⋆(w)≥(1−γ)𝖣ν(w∥wπ).\mathcal{S}^{\star}(w)\geq(1-\gamma)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi}). (S61)
Proof of Lemma S21.

Finiteness of 𝖣ν(w+∥v)\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w^{+}\|v) implies that w+w^{+} vanishes off the common support of ww and vv. Every integrand below therefore vanishes there. Expanding the three generalized-KL terms and canceling their linear parts gives

𝖣ν(w∥v)−𝖣ν(w+∥v)+𝖣ν(w+∥w)\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|v)-\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w^{+}\|v)+\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w^{+}\|w) =𝔼ν​[w​log⁡wv−w+​log⁡w+v+w+​log⁡w+w]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[w\log\frac{w}{v}-w^{+}\log\frac{w^{+}}{v}+w^{+}\log\frac{w^{+}}{w}\right] (S62)
=𝔼ν​[(w−w+)​log⁡wv].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[(w-w^{+})\log\frac{w}{v}\right].

The final expression in (S62) is the left-hand side of (S60), so that identity follows. To derive (S61), set v=wπv=w^{\pi}. By (S1) and (S4), this expression is 𝒮⋆​(w)\mathcal{S}^{\star}(w). Now use ℬπ∗​wπ=wπ\mathcal{B}_{\pi}^{\ast}w^{\pi}=w^{\pi} in Lemma S20. By that lemma, the middle divergence in (S60) is at most γ𝖣ν(w∥wπ)\gamma\mathsf{D}_{\nu}(w\|w^{\pi}), while the final divergence is nonnegative. Thus, (S61) follows. ∎

K.2.  Target-relative ratio bounds

Write

For (S65), set t=p/qt=p/q when q>0q>0. After division by qq, the difference between the right- and left-hand sides is

t​log⁡t−2​t+2​t=2​t​{t​log⁡t−t+1}≥0.t\log t-2t+2\sqrt{t}=2\sqrt{t}\{\sqrt{t}\log\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t}+1\}\geq 0.

When q>0q>0, the case p=0p=0 follows by continuity. When q=0q=0, finiteness of the right-hand side requires p=0p=0 under the convention in (S2), and both sides vanish. ∎

Remark S33 (L2L^{2}-normalized pairwise critics).

Proposition S7 shows that unnormalized pairwise-difference critics without penalization can fail under candidate-class misspecification. A population oracle inequality can also be obtained using L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-normalized pairwise differences, but finite-sample guarantees require additional control of empirical normalization.

To see this, define ψi​j:=hi​j/‖hi​j‖2,ν\psi_{ij}:=h_{ij}/\|h_{ij}\|_{2,\nu} when ‖hi​j‖2,ν>0\|h_{ij}\|_{2,\nu}>0, and ψi​j:=0\psi_{ij}:=0 otherwise. Under Conditions A2 and B5, any minimizer i~norm\widetilde{i}_{\mathrm{norm}} of maxj⁡|⟨ψi​j,Qi−ℬπ​Qi⟩ν|\max_{j}|\langle\psi_{ij},Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i}\rangle_{\nu}| satisfies the population oracle bound in Theorem S6. Indeed, take k=k⋆k=k^{\star} and write y:=‖Δk‖2,νy:=\|\Delta_{k}\|_{2,\nu}, u:=‖hi~norm,k‖2,νu:=\|h_{\widetilde{i}_{\mathrm{norm}},k}\|_{2,\nu}, and b:=‖Qk−ℬπ​Qk‖2,νb:=\|Q_{k}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{k}\|_{2,\nu}. The score of candidate kk is at most bb, whereas the score of the selected candidate is at least κν​u−b\kappa_{\nu}u-b. Optimality therefore gives u≤2​b/κνu\leq 2b/\kappa_{\nu}, and the triangle inequality yields the stated bound.

Finite-sample guarantees with empirical normalization require control of empirical norms relative to their population counterparts. Rescaling a difference alone rescales its moment and norm equally; the difficulty is concentration on rarely observed states. Sup-norm–L2L^{2} interpolation bounds quantify this concentration. For empirical standard-deviation normalization, these bounds apply to centered critics. Appendix O gives a concentration lemma, examples for linear and smooth function classes, and an oracle inequality for normalized-difference LSTD-Tournament.

L.2.2. Concentration of the unweighted scores

The Bellman equation and the triangle inequality give the bound with Lν^=1+γ​Cν^,πL_{\widehat{\nu}}=1+\gamma\sqrt{C_{\widehat{\nu},\pi}}. Also, ⟨f,(I−γ​Pπ)​f⟩ν^≥(1−γ​Cν^,π)​‖f‖2,ν^2\langle f,(I-\gamma P_{\pi})f\rangle_{\widehat{\nu}}\geq(1-\gamma\sqrt{C_{\widehat{\nu},\pi}})\|f\|_{2,\widehat{\nu}}^{2}, which proves the sufficient condition for fitted-weight coercivity.

Appendix N Unnormalized LSTD-Tournament under misspecification

We describe LSTDQ and establish a misspecification oracle inequality for the LSTD-Tournament selector of Liu et al. (2025, Equation (10)). Their realizable guarantee bounds policy-value error through a uniform value-function bound; here we study L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) error relative to the best candidate.

N.1.  Algorithm and oracle guarantee

For a feature map ϕ:𝒮×𝒜→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, least-squares temporal-difference QQ-learning (LSTDQ) estimates the linear approximation Qθ=ϕ⊤​θQ_{\theta}=\phi^{\top}\theta by solving empirical Bellman moment equations (Lagoudakis and Parr, 2003):

A^:=ℙn,Q​[ϕ⁡(X)​{ϕ⁡(X)−γ⁡(π​ϕ)​(S′)}⊤],b^:=ℙn,Q​[ϕ⁡(X)​R],θ^=A^−1​b^,\widehat{A}:=\mathbb{P}_{n,Q}\!\left[\phi(X)\{\phi(X)-\gamma(\pi\phi)(S^{\prime})\}^{\top}\right],\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{b}:=\mathbb{P}_{n,Q}[\phi(X)R],\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{\theta}=\widehat{A}^{-1}\widehat{b},

when A^\widehat{A} is invertible. Here ℙn,Q\mathbb{P}_{n,Q} denotes the validation-sample average, and π\pi acts on each coordinate of ϕ\phi. LSTD-Tournament uses ϕi​j:=(Qi,Qj)⊤\phi_{ij}:=(Q_{i},Q_{j})^{\top} for each candidate pair. For candidate ii, the corresponding LSTD moment score is maxℓ∈{i,j}⁡|ℙn,Q​[Qℓ​(X)​εi]|\max_{\ell\in\{i,j\}}|\mathbb{P}_{n,Q}[Q_{\ell}(X)\varepsilon_{i}]|, where εi:=Qi​(X)−R−γ⁡(π​Qi)​(S′)\varepsilon_{i}:=Q_{i}(X)-R-\gamma(\pi Q_{i})(S^{\prime}). Taking the largest pairwise score gives the unnormalized selector

T^i:=maxj∈[K]⁡|m^i​j|,m^i​j:=ℙn,Q​[Qj​(X)​εi],i^LT∈arg​mini∈[K]⁡T^i.\widehat{T}_{i}:=\max_{j\in[K]}|\widehat{m}_{ij}|,\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{m}_{ij}:=\mathbb{P}_{n,Q}[Q_{j}(X)\varepsilon_{i}],\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{i}_{\mathrm{LT}}\in\argmin_{i\in[K]}\widehat{T}_{i}. (S130)

The criterion uses candidate functions as critics, absolute moments, and no critic penalty. It requires only empirical moments, without inverting the pairwise empirical matrices.

Condition on the training sample and retain the validation setup of Section 2.1 and Condition A1. Assume the conditional TD mean bound GQG_{Q} in Condition B2 and the TD noise bound in Condition B3, both for i∈[K]i\in[K]. Assume also Qπ∈L2​(ν)Q^{\pi}\in L^{2}(\nu) and 𝔼ν​|R|<∞\mathbb{E}_{\nu}|R|<\infty. Set

μi:=Qi−ℬπ​Qi,mi​j:=⟨Qj,μi⟩ν,Ti:=maxj∈[K]⁡|mi​j|.\mu_{i}:=Q_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{i},\hskip 18.49988ptm_{ij}:=\langle Q_{j},\mu_{i}\rangle_{\nu},\hskip 18.49988ptT_{i}:=\max_{j\in[K]}|m_{ij}|.

Let K≥2K\geq 2 and let k⋆∈arg​mini∈[K]⁡‖Qi−Qπ‖2,νk^{\star}\in\argmin_{i\in[K]}\|Q_{i}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu} index a best candidate. In addition to the existing conditions, impose the following:

  1. (LT1)

    Bounded candidate functions. There is a finite BQ>0B_{Q}>0 such that maxi∈[K]⁡|Qi​(X)|≤BQ\max_{i\in[K]}|Q_{i}(X)|\leq B_{Q}, ν\nu-almost surely.

  2. (LT2)

    LSTD moments along oracle-comparison directions. For ϕi​k⋆:=(Qi,Qk⋆)⊤\phi_{ik^{\star}}:=(Q_{i},Q_{k^{\star}})^{\top}, define

    Ai​k⋆:=𝔼ν​[ϕi​k⋆​(X)​{ϕi​k⋆​(X)−γ⁡(Pπ​ϕi​k⋆)​(X)}⊤].A_{ik^{\star}}:=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[\phi_{ik^{\star}}(X)\{\phi_{ik^{\star}}(X)-\gamma(P_{\pi}\phi_{ik^{\star}})(X)\}^{\top}\right].

    There is a constant sLT​(k⋆)>0s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})>0 such that

    ∑ℓ∈{i,k⋆}⟨Qℓ,(I−γ​Pπ)​hi​k⋆⟩ν2≥2​sLT​(k⋆)2,κLT​(k⋆):=sLT​(k⋆)2​BQ2.\sum_{\ell\in\{i,k^{\star}\}}\left\langle Q_{\ell},(I-\gamma P_{\pi})h_{ik^{\star}}\right\rangle_{\nu}^{2}\geq 2s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})^{2},\hskip 18.49988pt\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star}):=\frac{s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})}{2B_{Q}^{2}}. (S131)

    The inequality is required for every ii with ‖hi​k⋆‖2,ν>0\|h_{ik^{\star}}\|_{2,\nu}>0.

The full singular-value bound mini≠k⋆⁡σmin​(Ai​k⋆)≥sLT​(k⋆)>0\min_{i\neq k^{\star}}\sigma_{\min}(A_{ik^{\star}})\geq s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})>0, analogous to that assumed by Liu et al. (2025), is sufficient for Condition LT2. Indeed, for v=(1,−1)⊤v=(1,-1)^{\top}, the left-hand side of (S131) equals

‖Ai​k⋆​v‖22≥σmin​(Ai​k⋆)2​‖v‖22≥2​sLT​(k⋆)2.\|A_{ik^{\star}}v\|_{2}^{2}\geq\sigma_{\min}(A_{ik^{\star}})^{2}\|v\|_{2}^{2}\geq 2s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})^{2}.

Our condition is weaker, requiring only that the Bellman moments along the candidate–oracle difference do not both vanish. In particular, it allows the pairwise LSTD matrices to be singular.

Theorem S36 (LSTD-Tournament oracle inequality under misspecification).

Under the conditions above, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), conditional on training, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the selector in (S130) satisfies

‖Qi^LT−Qπ‖2,ν≤\displaystyle\|Q_{\widehat{i}_{\mathrm{LT}}}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu}\leq{} ‖Qk⋆−Qπ‖2,ν+2κLT​(k⋆)​‖Qk⋆−ℬπ​Qk⋆‖2,ν\displaystyle\|Q_{k^{\star}}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu}+\frac{2}{\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})}\|Q_{k^{\star}}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{k^{\star}}\|_{2,\nu}
+2​CM​(GQ+σQ)κLT​(k⋆)​{rn,δ+rn,δ2},rn,δ:=log⁡(18​K/δ)n​gb,\displaystyle+\frac{2C_{\mathrm{M}}(G_{Q}+\sigma_{Q})}{\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})}\{r_{n,\delta}+r_{n,\delta}^{2}\},\hskip 18.49988ptr_{n,\delta}:=\sqrt{\frac{\log(18K/\delta)}{ng_{b}}}, (S132)

where CMC_{\mathrm{M}} is the universal constant in Lemma S19. Every population minimizer i~LT∈arg​mini⁡Ti\widetilde{i}_{\mathrm{LT}}\in\argmin_{i}T_{i} satisfies the same bound without the validation term.

If n​gb≥log⁡(18​K/δ)ng_{b}\geq\log(18K/\delta), the validation term in (S132) is at most {4​CM​(GQ+σQ)/κLT​(k⋆)}​log⁡(18​K/δ)/(n​gb)\{4C_{\mathrm{M}}(G_{Q}+\sigma_{Q})/\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})\}\sqrt{\log(18K/\delta)/(ng_{b})}. A multiplicative best-candidate bound additionally requires ‖Qk⋆−ℬπ​Qk⋆‖2,ν≤Lν​‖Qk⋆−Qπ‖2,ν\|Q_{k^{\star}}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{k^{\star}}\|_{2,\nu}\leq L_{\nu}\|Q_{k^{\star}}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu}. Under this condition, the first two terms become

{1+2​LνκLT​(k⋆)}​mini​‖Qi−Qπ‖2,ν.\left\{1+\frac{2L_{\nu}}{\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k^{\star})}\right\}\min_{i}\|Q_{i}-Q^{\pi}\|_{2,\nu}.

One-step concentrability with Cν,π=‖d⁡(ν​Pπ)/d​ν‖∞<∞C_{\nu,\pi}=\|\mathrm{d}(\nu P_{\pi})/\mathrm{d}\nu\|_{\infty}<\infty is sufficient, with Lν=1+γ​Cν,πL_{\nu}=1+\gamma\sqrt{C_{\nu,\pi}}, by Jensen’s inequality and Qk⋆−ℬπ​Qk⋆=(I−γ​Pπ)​(Qk⋆−Qπ)Q_{k^{\star}}-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q_{k^{\star}}=(I-\gamma P_{\pi})(Q_{k^{\star}}-Q^{\pi}).

N.2.  Moment identification and validation deviations

Throughout the proofs below, write k=k⋆k=k^{\star}.

Lemma S37 (LSTD moment identification).

Under Conditions LT1 and LT2, for every i≠ki\neq k,

‖Qi−Qk‖2,ν≤1κLT​(k)​BQ​maxℓ∈{i,k}​|mi​ℓ−mk​ℓ|.\|Q_{i}-Q_{k}\|_{2,\nu}\leq\frac{1}{\kappa_{\mathrm{LT}}(k)B_{Q}}\max_{\ell\in\{i,k\}}|m_{i\ell}-m_{k\ell}|. (S133)
Proof.

Since Qj−γ​Pπ​Qj=μj+r∈L1​(ν)Q_{j}-\gamma P_{\pi}Q_{j}=\mu_{j}+r\in L^{1}(\nu) and the candidates are bounded, all matrix and moment entries below are finite. If ‖Qi−Qk‖2,ν=0\|Q_{i}-Q_{k}\|_{2,\nu}=0, the inequality holds directly. Otherwise, the difference is covered by Condition LT2. Write B=BQB=B_{Q} and s=sLT​(k)s=s_{\mathrm{LT}}(k). For v=(1,−1)⊤v=(1,-1)^{\top}, linearity gives

Ai​k​v=𝔼ν​[ϕi​k​(I−γ​Pπ)​(Qi−Qk)]=(mi​i−mk​imi​k−mk​k).A_{ik}v=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[\phi_{ik}(I-\gamma P_{\pi})(Q_{i}-Q_{k})]=\begin{pmatrix}m_{ii}-m_{ki}\\ m_{ik}-m_{kk}\end{pmatrix}.

The candidate bound and ‖Ai​k​v‖2≥s​‖v‖2\|A_{ik}v\|_{2}\geq s\|v\|_{2} imply

‖Qi−Qk‖2,ν≤2​B​‖v‖2≤2​Bs​‖Ai​k​v‖2≤2​Bs​‖Ai​k​v‖∞.\|Q_{i}-Q_{k}\|_{2,\nu}\leq\sqrt{2}B\|v\|_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}B}{s}\|A_{ik}v\|_{2}\leq\frac{2B}{s}\|A_{ik}v\|_{\infty}.

Substituting (S131) proves (S133). ∎

Lemma S38 (Validation moment deviations).

Under the sampling and TD conditions of Theorem S36 and Condition LT1, define

𝒫k:={(k,j):j∈[K]}∪{(i,i),(i,k):i≠k}.\mathcal{P}_{k}:=\{(k,j):j\in[K]\}\cup\{(i,i),(i,k):i\neq k\}.

For every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), conditional on training, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

max(i,j)∈𝒫k⁡|m^i​j−mi​j|≤τn,δ,τn,δ:=CM​BQ​(GQ+σQ)​{rn,δ+rn,δ2}.\max_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{k}}|\widehat{m}_{ij}-m_{ij}|\leq\tau_{n,\delta},\hskip 18.49988pt\tau_{n,\delta}:=C_{\mathrm{M}}B_{Q}(G_{Q}+\sigma_{Q})\{r_{n,\delta}+r_{n,\delta}^{2}\}. (S134)

Proof of Theorem S36.

For every n≥8n\geq 8, there exist a single-action MDP with γ=0\gamma=0 and two candidates, all rewards and candidates taking values in [0,3][0,3], satisfying Conditions A1, A2, B2, B3, and B5 with gb=κν=1g_{b}=\kappa_{\nu}=1, HQ=GQ=3H_{Q}=G_{Q}=3, and σQ=1\sigma_{Q}=1, such that k⋆=1k^{\star}=1, C1≤5C_{1}\leq\sqrt{5}, and

ℱnd:={Qi:i∈[K]}∪{hi​j:i,j∈[K],i≠j},Λnd:=maxf∈ℱnd‖f−𝔼ν​f‖∞2σν​(f)2.\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{nd}}:=\{Q_{i}:i\in[K]\}\cup\{h_{ij}:i,j\in[K],\ i\neq j\},\hskip 18.49988pt\Lambda_{\mathrm{nd}}:=\max_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{nd}}}\frac{\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}f\|_{\infty}^{2}}{\sigma_{\nu}(f)^{2}}.

Appendix P Adjoint LSTD-Tournament for occupancy-ratio selection

P.1.  Algorithm and oracle guarantee

Adjoint LSTD-Tournament selects among occupancy-ratio candidates w1,…,wMw_{1},\ldots,w_{M} fitted independently of the validation data. Let ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} average over validation transitions and ℙm0\mathbb{P}_{m}^{0} over initial draws from d0d_{0}. For each ordered pair, compute

m^i​j\displaystyle\widehat{m}_{ij} :=ℙn​[wi​(X)​{wj​(X)−γ⁡(π​wj)​(S′)}]−(1−γ)​ℙm0​[wj],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[w_{i}(X)\{w_{j}(X)-\gamma(\pi w_{j})(S^{\prime})\}\right]-(1-\gamma)\mathbb{P}_{m}^{0}[w_{j}],
T^i\displaystyle\widehat{T}_{i} :=maxj∈[M]⁡|m^i​j|,i^ALT∈arg​mini∈[M]⁡T^i.\displaystyle:=\max_{j\in[M]}|\widehat{m}_{ij}|,\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{i}_{\mathrm{ALT}}\in\argmin_{i\in[M]}\widehat{T}_{i}. (S141)

Ties may be resolved by candidate order. If initial moments are known exactly, replace ℙm0​[wj]\mathbb{P}_{m}^{0}[w_{j}] by 𝔼d0​[wj]\mathbb{E}_{d_{0}}[w_{j}]. The selector uses the candidates themselves as critics, absolute moments, and no critic penalty. Let mi​jm_{ij} and Ti=maxj⁡|mi​j|T_{i}=\max_{j}|m_{ij}| denote the population counterparts.

Appendix Q Additional related work

Section 1.3 compares PBV with existing Bellman validation methods and LSTD-Tournament. This appendix discusses OPE model selection, occupancy-ratio estimation, supervised aggregation, and statistical inverse problems.

Model selection for QQ-functions and occupancy ratios. Existing OPE model-selection methods have focused primarily on QQ-functions, replacing the unavailable supervised loss with structured Bellman criteria. BErMin estimates Bellman error with complexity penalties; BVFT and BVFT-PE use projected Bellman errors over candidate-dependent state aggregations; and ModBE uses relative square-loss tests for nested model classes (Farahmand and Szepesvári, 2011; Xie and Jiang, 2021; Zhang and Jiang, 2021; Lee et al., 2022). Supervised Bellman validation instead regresses the one-step TD target on the current state and action separately for each candidate. Duality-based Residual Estimation learns residual critics and selects among critic configurations on an additional split (Zitovsky et al., 2023; Miyaguchi, 2026). PBV instead constructs critics directly from the candidates, avoiding candidate-dependent projection, nestedness, and auxiliary critic fitting.

Model-selection targets in OPE.

Model selection arises at several levels in off-policy evaluation. One line of work selects or combines scalar value estimates, including MAGIC, SWITCH, shrinkage estimators, SLOPE, proxy-task and cross-validation methods, and OPERA (Thomas and Brunskill, 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Su et al., 2020a; Su et al., 2020b; Udagawa et al., 2023; Cief et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2024). A second line uses OPE to rank policies or tune complete offline-RL pipelines (Irpan et al., 2019; Paine et al., 2020; Tang and Wiens, 2021; Yang et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2022). Zhang and Jiang (2021) primarily study offline policy selection but also use BVFT-PE to select among candidate QπQ^{\pi} estimates for a fixed policy. We instead study nuisance selection for a fixed target policy. From finite classes of candidates fitted independently of the validation data, we select the QQ-function or occupancy-ratio estimate used for OPE. This differs from selecting scalar value estimates or policies because neither nuisance is observed, so their target losses are not directly available.

Occupancy-ratio estimation and selection.

Marginalized importance sampling, DICE methods, and minimax weight learning estimate discounted occupancy ratios from adjoint Bellman equations, typically using prescribed ratio and critic classes (Xie et al., 2019; Nachum et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Uehara et al., 2020; Uehara et al., 2021). FORE is an occupancy-ratio analogue of FQE that estimates the ratio through fitted adjoint Bellman recursion without requiring Bellman completeness (van der Laan and Kallus, 2026), while FORC is a related finite-horizon method that does require Bellman completeness (Huang et al., 2023; Huang and Jiang, 2024). These methods construct an occupancy-ratio estimate within a specified function class. A-PBV instead selects post hoc among already-fitted candidates using pairwise log-ratio critics and Hellinger-penalized adjoint Bellman scores.

Supervised model selection and aggregation.

In supervised prediction, held-out outcomes make the risk of a fixed candidate directly estimable. Cross-validation uses this risk to select algorithms or tuning parameters, while stacking and Super Learner combine candidates using cross-validated predictions (Stone, 1974; Wolpert, 1992; van der Laan and Dudoit, 2003; van der Laan et al., 2007). Model-selection aggregation instead seeks to match the best element of a finite dictionary; under squared loss, Q-aggregation attains sharp oracle inequalities with logarithmic remainders (Dai et al., 2012; Lan and Syrgkanis, 2024). These supervised criteria are unavailable here because neither QπQ^{\pi} nor wπw^{\pi} is observed, squared temporal-difference error is not a valid target loss, and offline-distribution Bellman moments need not control target-policy error. PBV instead constructs directly estimable pairwise criteria and selects a candidate from the fitted class rather than forming an aggregate.

Model selection in linear inverse problems.

Related model-selection challenges arise in statistical linear inverse problems, where instability of the inverse operator motivates operator-dependent risk estimates and penalties (Cavalier et al., 2002; Abramovich et al., 2018). For example, Regularized DeepIV uses an out-of-sample Tikhonov criterion to obtain oracle guarantees under misspecification in nonparametric instrumental-variable regression (Li et al., 2024). In general, small forward error need not control structural error without regularization and source or link conditions. Here, the Bellman evaluation operator is a γ\sqrt{\gamma}-contraction in L2​(dπ,γ)L^{2}(d_{\pi,\gamma}), while the adjoint Bellman update contracts generalized KL divergence by a factor of γ\gamma. These contractions convert pairwise Bellman moments into target-error bounds without a Tikhonov bias–variance choice or inverse-problem source conditions. IW-PBV requires coverage and occupancy-ratio accuracy, A-PBV requires bounded ratio candidates and bounded pairwise log ratios, and unweighted PBV requires a coercivity condition under the offline distribution.
